maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext:
A
week ago, on April 14, I asked a question of the Prime Minister with regard to a reported United States embargo on agricultural products. Since that time President Eisenhower has asked the tariff commission to give consideration to the continuance of the embargo against certain Canadian dairy products, such as flaxseed, linseed, and the like. What reply has the United States given

Inquiries of the Ministry to the two notes of protest to which reference was made at that time? What further action does the government contemplate in order to remove what appears to be an injustice by the United States toward Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and
Commerce is prepared to answer my hon. friend's question.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to my hon. friend's question of a week ago, reports have been received of discussions in the United States of possible restrictions upon the importation of oats and feeds. It is understood that these reports have arisen out of the appearance of the secretary of agriculture before a subcommittee of the Senate where general proposals are at present being subjected to study and investigation. To the best of my knowledge, no conclusions or recommendations to congress have as yet emerged nor is this subject dealt with as yet in draft legislation. In these circumstances, it is not appropriate at present for the Canadian government to make official representations or protests. I am, of course, fully aware of the importance to Canada of the trade in oats and feed grains. The numerous hearings before various committees of the United States congress, which are studying agricultural programs, are being closely followed here. The United States government is well aware of Canada's concern and of the importance of trade between the two countries in agricultural products. The Prime Minister is planning to visit the United States in the near future. When he is in Washington he will have occasion to refer to some of the important questions of trade relationships between Canada and the United States as well as to some of the questions affecting world trade and financial relationships.
With respect to embargoes and restrictions on the importation of dairy products into the United States, the government of Canada has made official representations to the government of the United States on a number of occasions, which have been publicly announced in both countries. These representations have taken the form of notes to convey the Canadian point of view, but so worded as not to require replies. The most recent of these representations was a note delivered on February 10 of the present year which referred explicitly to Canada's serious concern respecting import restrictions in the United States upon dairy products. This same subject has been raised by Canadian delegations to successive sessions of the con-

tracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. In addition, official Canadian representatives in Washington have frequently had occasion to refer to these restrictions.
I think that answers the second question of my hon. friend as well as the first question.

maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? I noticed that in the minister's statement, which was full, he said that the notes in protest were couched in such language as not to require replies. What was the reason that the notes were couched in that way? I ask that question as a matter of interest. I wondered why the United States was not asked to clarify the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: These notes had reference to the current legislation, and I think that if we were to receive a note from another government about legislation that we were contemplating we would not answer that note. It was felt the subject was one about which we could not expect an answer, but about which the Canadian views should be forcibly presented.

maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that the last communication with Washington was on February 10?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: Oh, no; as a matter of fact, representations are being made almost every day. For example, at my request our chief delegate to the international wheat conference called on the Department of Agriculture and made protests on the subject matter that I have just discussed. He discussed the matter very fully with officers of the Department of Agriculture and also ways and means of correcting a situation that is disturbing to the Americans. The two countries are in such close contact in these matters that a formal note is not the only means of communication. Our ambassador and our officials are in constant touch with their opposite numbers in Washington.

maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: Has the government com sidered any legislation similar to the "Buy American" legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: REPORTED EMBARGO BY UNITED STATES AGAINST OATS AND FEEDS  DAIRY PRODUCTS
speechtext: No.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 48, respecting food, drugs, cosmetics and therapeutic devices.

Can the minister explain the
bill?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is the minister going to
make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
This bill, which seeks a
revision of one of the older statutes in our country, provides for a revision of the act and the consolidation of some of the sections and introduces some new features that will strengthen the measure. The bill was first introduced in the other place, and has had a full hearing in the committee on health and welfare of that place, giving an opportunity to industry generally to make representations in connection with some proposals that are now embodied in the measure before the house.
The Canadian Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Allied Beauty Equipment Manufacturers Association and the Ottawa Truss Company were among those national trade organizations that made representations in connection with this measure. The present bill, as I say, is a revision and consolidation of certain provisions; and it seeks to remove certain anomalies which, in the light of experience during the last twenty years, it has been thought desirable to introduce.
The purpose of the bill of course is to protect the Canadian people in matters of health, as well as against fraud in the manufacturing and sale of foods and drugs. The administration of the measure depends upon the co-operation that the officials of the department are able to enjoy with industry. I cannot speak too highly of the co-operation we have had from industry generally in the administration of this act. There is no basic or essential difference in the present measure from the existing act except in a few particulars, one or two of which I shall point out. The bill is concerned with the prohibition of things that are injurious to health and that are unfit for use, and with the prevention of deception in the manufacture and sale of goods consumed by the public.

Food and Drugs Act
One important provision I should like to outline is the one to remove from ministerial power the discretion that now exists with respect to the forfeiture of goods. At the present time the powers of the minister under the act are great, and I have felt for some time that there should be a limit placed upon those powers, and that any interference with the use of property should be only after the exercise of judicial processes.
For example it frequently happens that goods having a substantial financial value are seized and forfeiture ensues, not upon a ruling by a court, but first through seizures by inspectors, followed by a decision of the minister in the exercise of this discretion, and based upon analyses made by an analyst. It has been thought that hereafter, except by the consent of the owner, no forfeiture of goods should take place unless there has been determination by judicial process as to whether or not the goods are in conformity with the act, and as to whether or not under the circumstances the forfeiture should be undertaken.
I think this is an important change in administration, and follows the due process of law clause in corresponding legislation in other countries.
This act is one of the important measures on our statute books. It affects the welfare and health of every person in this country, and I commend the measure to the house.

Mr. Speaker, I think the minister's explanation has cleared up the situation. While we agree with the principle of the bill I would suggest that those parts we wish to criticize should be taken up clause by clause in committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the
introduction of this measure, and feel that its importance merited a longer statement than the minister has given this morning. No doubt he will make up for that when we get into committee on the various clauses.
As he has pointed out, it is extremely important for the protection of the health of the Canadian people that there be legislation of this kind, and also that its administration be carried out effectively. We wish to join with the minister in the tribute he paid to those who have had charge of the enforcement of this legislation. We are glad to note that the bill does in fact include provisions that will strengthen the hands of those who have that task.
I note in a number of places in the bill a new phrase which reads: "manufactured,
tMr. Martin.]
prepared, preserved, packaged or stored in unsanitary conditions". While I have quoted it from only one point in the bill, it appears in several places. My interpretation would be that the inclusion of that new phrase in a number of places in the bill would seem to give the inspectors who operate under the legislation wider powers to make sure that foods, drugs, cosmetics, appliances or devices which could be injurious to the health of the people because of the conditions under which they are produced, will not be allowed on the market. It is made clear in the bill not only that foods, drugs or devices themselves must not be impure or adulterated in any way, but that they must not come from any place which in any way could be considered unsanitary.
We are glad to note this attempt to tighten up the administration of this legislation. We feel that those in charge of it have been doing a good job, and we are glad to give them the further provisions contained in the bill.
We are also glad to note that there is a new phraseology in some sections of the bill dealing with the question of deception. As I understand it, once this new bill becomes law it will be unlawful for persons to advertise drugs, appliances or devices as having therapeutic or healing effects. Indeed the whole aim of the legislation as I understand it is to make sure that people who are suffering from certain diseases or disorders will not be deluded by false advertising, and as a result of that delusion be induced to stay away from physicians or doctors whom they should see.
We think this is all to the good. We are pleased with the progress science is making in all branches, particularly in the medical field. But we do believe that the people should be protected against any false assertions made in advertising. We know there are many occasions when the sellers of certain products are tempted to make all they can out of those products by advertising in very glowing terms.
I would hope that when we are discussing the sections of the bill the minister would speak in greater detail. At this point however I wish to say simply that we welcome these steps.
One other thought occurs to me-and with this I shall have concluded my remarks at this stage of debate-and it is that in view of the fact that this measure provides for a clearer and greater supervision over drugs, appliances and devices to be made available, the Department of National Health and Welfare should extend the list of drugs and appliances it recommends to the Minister of

Finance (Mr. Abbott) or to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) for income tax deductibility.
I have no intention of developing that subject into what Your Honour might classify as a budget speech, and therefore would rule out of order. But it does seem to me that the subject does go along with the one now before us-and I am glad to note that the minister nods his head affirmatively. As parliament specifies greater control over drugs, appliances and devices, I am suggesting that on that basis the list of those allowed as deductible for income tax purposes should be greatly extended.
With those remarks, I conclude by saying that we welcome this bill and, so far as it goes, we heartily support it.

Mr. Speaker, I have taken a great interest in this subject for a number of years and I want to say how pleased I am to see this bill being introduced by the minister. However, like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I was somewhat surprised that the minister's statement on such an important piece of legislation was conspicuous for its brevity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The minister does not usually enjoy that reputation.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is what made it such a surprise.

It was the exception that proved the rule. This indicates a definite stiffening of the pure food and drugs laws of this country and as such we in this group certainly welcome it. Since the major amendments of 1927 there have been great changes in manufacturing practices and procedures, in packaging and so on. Many new drugs and synthetic compounds have been put on the market and I think it is high time that this legislation was introduced.
Like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, we want to pay a tribute to the excellent work done by the officials of the pure food and drugs division of the department. A great deal of scientific and painstaking work is carried on by this division behind the scenes, quite often with little public recognition. However, I think more and more people are becoming aware of the excellent pure food and drugs division we have in Canada at this time.
The minister's department has received excellent co-operation from the Canadian Association of Consumers. These women have taken the time to carry out investigations
Food and Drugs Act
in the various cities and small communities of this country and they make their recommendations and complaints to the division and have contributed a great deal toward the improvement and administration of the act. The development of this act and its amendments have been the result of considerable co-operation between the minister, his officials and the consuming public.
I have noticed a growing interest in these matters. I remember when I first came to Ottawa in 1945 there seemed to be few people who had any knowledge of this act and of the work being done by the division.
I find that that situation has changed. Letters that I receive indicate an intelligent and widespread interest in the work and I have no hesitation in saying again that the minister's officials in this department are doing an excellent and an increasingly important job for this country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Interpretation.

The definition of "analyst" is given as follows:
(b) "analyst" means any person designated as a food and drug analyst under subsection (2) of section 24.
Section 24, subsection 2, reads:
The governor in council may designate as an analyst or inspector any person on the staff of the department for such time as that person is employed in the department or for such time during the period of such employment as he may direct.
There is nothing there to indicate that the analyst must possess certain qualifications.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I think my friend will appreciate that no one would be appointed as an analyst who did not have the qualifications. I think that implication is carried in the measure.
Would it not be better to have the word "qualified" or something of that nature in there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is not usual in legislation of this kind to put in such an adjective. This was cleared by justice. No one would be appointed who did not have the necessary qualifications and to have the word "qualified" would not of itself provide any guarantee. I assure my hon. friend that this is the usual draftsmanship.

Is it the intention to have an analyst in each province? At the present time there is no analyst in Newfoundland. If medicines come in that have to be

Food and Drugs Act
analysed, they must be returned to Halifax for analysis and then sent back to Newfoundland. It is very awkward and causes considerable delay.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That matter is under
consideration.
What has happened to the food and drugs act in Newfoundland since 1949? That act was based on the English law and we had inspectors operating under it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: We have carried on there just as we have carried on in the rest of the country. We have appointed inspectors.
Will there be any difference when this bill is passed?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It will make this difference: We think the measure is an improvement over the existing act, although we think the existing act is an excellent measure. The advantages that will accrue to the rest of Canada will accrue to Newfoundland.
The minister is going to take the power under this act to make regulations that will cover many varieties of things.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: He has that power now.
Those will continue in force?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.

Paragraph (j) reads:
"Minister" means the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I cannot understand why that definition is put there when it does not mean anything. The minister cannot be ubiquitous and be in every province at the same time. Prosecutions may be going on in every province at the same time.
Paul gets around.

Should not the definition include the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister and so on? I notice that when we were dealing with the foot-and-mouth disease the word "minister" was used when the minister did not know anything about it for two months. Is not the general interpretation section in conflict with this, in that it provides that the minister means the deputy minister, during the minister's absence, or his assistant or any other person who may be designated.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I can only say that this is
the usual practice. The minister in charge of a department is responsible for the acts of his officials as well as his own. This is 
the formal designation that is usual in Anglo-American communities and I am sure on reflection it will commend itself to the high legal attainments of the hon. gentleman.

I do not
think that that explanation covers it. Perhaps I may be permitted to refer to section 12, which reads:
No person shall sell any drug described in schedule C or D unless the minister has, in prescribed form and manner, indicated that the premises in which the drug was manufactured and the process and conditions of manufacture therein are suitable to ensure that the drug will not be unsafe for use.
That does not mean that the minister is going to look at every premises where foods or drugs are being manufactured or displayed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The word "minister" is used in the same sense as the word "crown" is used for other purposes.

I understand that at the
present time there are quite a number of patent medicines coming in from the United States and other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Could we deal with that
under the appropriate section?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-No food, drug, etc., to be advertised or sold as a treatment, etc., for certain diseases.

This section reads:
No person shall advertise any food, drug, cosmetic or device to the general public as a treatment, preventative or cure for any of the diseases, disorders or abnormal physical states mentioned in schedule A.
In looking over schedule A, I see a number of diseases and so-called diseases mentioned there about which I have often seen advertisements. One in particular is obesity, and we need not look far for an example of a person who has responded to treatment. But we frequently see advertisements, especially in movie magazines and that sort of thing, addressed principally to young ladies and telling them how they may reduce their figures and get a more admirable one. Is it going to be an offence to recommend that a person should adopt the practice of slimming, eat Hollywood bread and more vegetables and adopt a change of diet?
I want to make a reference to some less conspicuous diseases. I notice that in the schedule venereal diseases and sexual impotence are mentioned. There is a provision in the Criminal Code which makes advertisements of cures for these particular conditions punishable. Another one is influenza.

I am very glad to see it referred to here because I remember reading an article in the Reader's Digest two years ago about a certain brand of pills that were a sure cure for influenza. I remember recommending them to one of my colleagues and taking some myself. I fell asleep with the window open and the temperature at 10 below zero and woke up with a more severe attack of influenza than when I went to sleep. I certainly think that the proper thing for a person to do is to go to a doctor when he feels ill and not rely on articles, even in such a prominent publication as the Reader's Digest.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: This is an important section. In many respects it is perhaps the most important in the bill. My hon. friend has referred to one of the diseases mentioned in schedule A. I must say first of all that the particular item was in the schedule long before the recent historical developments in my own person took place. But apart altogether from my own achievements in that particular -and I do not want to be personal except for the fact that my hon. friend has referred to me as exhibit A-I simply want to say that obesity is included in the schedule on the advice of my technical people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The minister used to be a fairly substantial exhibit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Lanark will be pleased to give my hon. friend some advice. Obesity is a very serious thing. All sorts of advertising are being carried on in this country telling people how to reduce, and as doctors know that can be a fairly serious matter if not properly done and under proper supervision. No one should resort to the process of dieting without first consulting his doctor. There are pills and other things being advertised that are very dangerous. It is for that reason that obesity is included along with other diseases like cancer.
The main purpose of the provision is not to discourage initiative in industry or in professional activity but, having in mind the public interest, to make sure that no one shall advertise any food, drug, cosmetic or device as a treatment, preventive or cure for any of the serious diseases and conditions described in schedule A. This measure does not seek to disturb people advertising their wares, but they shall not advertise them as a treatment for those conditions. For instance, there are certain bodies in this country advertising preparations as a treatment and cure for cancer. That is a fraud on the public, and this measure seeks to prevent that. It does not mean that medical men may not recommend certain
Food and Drugs Act
things, but vendors of nostrums shall not be permitted to carry on that practice. I know of the case of an official who works on the staff of the House of Commons and whose wife died of cancer a year ago. She was taking a certain pill that had been recommended to her by a practitioner who was not carrying out the responsibility of his high office. He recommended it to her. It was advertised as a treatment in a little publication that came to our attention. This woman did not go to see a doctor who might have given her assistance, although I do not know whether he could have in the light of her condition. The section will deal with this kind of situation, and I am sure the importance of the provision will commend itself to every hon. member.

I think the list is very well
chosen. I went over it carefully yesterday. Some of the diseases included in the list may look rather innocent, but there is a reason behind every single one. For instance, obesity may appear to be rather innocent. ' I am not going to refer to anybody who has received treatment, but I remember very well that a certain type of pill was sold, particularly on the other side of the border, which caused a lot of trouble and brought about some fatalities in this country. The list is well chosen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
It caused blindness and
cataracts.

Yes. There is an inclination
to advertise a cure for almost everything, and while some of these diseases may appear innocent there is a real reason behind their inclusion in the schedule. I congratulate the department on having gone so far, and in the future I think that the list can be enlarged. I do not say this as a physician apposed to certain cures. These are things for which I know it is impossible to advertise a cure, and it is a dangerous practice to do so.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Can the minister say where
the line is drawn with respect to this matter? I would think it would be clear that any advertisement that said specifically that such and such was a cure for such and such a disease would be illegal. What about the type of advertising that indulges in the before and after technique? Suppose some firm advertised by simply publishing two pictures of the minister, one before and one after, and said that he had done so and so. Would that be unlawful? Where is the line drawn?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That might be embarrassing
but it certainly would not be unlawful. If a company advertises a particular product as a treatment, cure or preventive, that is

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 4-Prohibited sales of food.
With respect to the word "adulterated", there does not seem to be a clear explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Perhaps I could explain. In the old act adulteration included (a), Cb) and (c) of section 4 as well as (a) in section 24. The word "adulteration" as used in section 4 is to be given the usual grammatical definition, the definition that would be found in any dictionary. If a court were called upon to construe what was meant by adulteration in this particular section it would give it the ordinary meaning. That is according to the rules of interpretation in law. This particular method was arrived at in the light of the experience we have had in some of our cases. If my hon. friend will look at section 24 (1) (a), he will see that by implication adulteration as used there means adding something that is a prescribed substance or withdrawing something that is a prescribed substance. The present arrangement arises out of our experience in the administration of this measure and it follows the practice in certain other countries.

The old definition, Mr. Chairman, is very good, but subsection (a) of section 24 does not fully cover the matter. The minister has cited the dictionary definition of adding or omitting something but I would suggest that the definition there be something like this:	That an article would
be deemed to be adulterated if something were added, subtracted or omitted lessening its therapeutic value or rendering it dangerous for human consumption.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
That would be all right but we consider adulteration as something not so severe as that. In our effort to maintain and operate standards there is not only the question of whether something is injurious to health but also the question of whether it is contrary to certain prescribed standards within the over-all plan. My hon. friend has asked that we give careful consideration 

to this, but may I assure him this represents the best thinking in food and drug law experience at the moment. I will give it further consideration in the light of further experience as suggested.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-Deception.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring up, under this section, a matter which affects a Hamilton processing firm with which the minister is thoroughly familiar. It concerns the sale on the market of a product known as oilless mayonnaise as against another article known as salad dressing. These people have been marketing this product for 16 years and it has popular acceptance on the market. It says:
Oilless mayonnaise-made of eggs, cream, sugar, vinegar, mustard, salt, spices and condiments.
There is no attempt there at any deception whatsoever. Anyone can read what is in the article and it has popular acceptance. I would like to protest very strongly against the department's action in trying to remove from the market an article which has popular consumer acceptance.
There was another Hamilton firm, as a matter of fact, which made oilless mayonnaise some time ago, but owing to pressure from the department they changed the name of their particular product and called it "Dressing Supreme". Mr. Chairman, that is just a lot of nonsense. If an article is a popular article and if it does no harm and is a wholesome product I cannot see any difference whether you call it a rose or a violet. It is still healthy. For the department to take the stand that under the term "mayonnaise" no product can be marketed unless oil is included is a lot of nonsense. As a matter of fact, I think that if you went back to the term "mayonnaise" in the broad sense you might describe it as something that was manufactured at the whim of a woman. There are no two cooks in the country who have exactly the same recipes for the foods which they prepare for their families.
I have had a good many cook-books in my house which had recipes for mayonnaise and for salad dressing and which required no oil whatever. There are some products on the market at the present time, under various trade names, which do not include oil and those apparently have the full approval of the department. I cannot see that the department has any right to force a manufacturer to remove from the market a product of this nature-particularly when you consider the amount of money which must go into the build-up of a trade name and the advertising which was necessary in

order to promote the sale of that article. In this case, after 16 years, the department decides that the description is a misnomer and they ask that the product be removed from sale. It does not seem to me, Mr. Chairman, to have anything to do with the health of this country whether any article is called salad dressing or mayonnaise, and if the public is fully aware of the ingredients I cannot agree that the department is correct in making such a stipulation. Apparently it has no such stipulation for other dressings but only on mayonnaise and salad dressings. They come in under B.07.034 and B.07.036, respectively, in the one case with 65 per cent vegetable oil and in the other case 35 per cent vegetable oil. I understand that these regulations were not enforced during the war for the simple reason that there was not sufficient vegetable oil. We do not know but what we will have to face that situation again. The department's stand seems to me to be entirely wrong and I want to protest most vigorously against their action in trying to force the manufacturer to remove from the market a healthful product which has had public acceptance for 16 years.

Mr. Chairman, I am taking into account the experience of the hon. member but she will remember that some of us also have had experience in marketing these products. I would like to say that she knows from her experience and I know that the definition of mayonnaise in the retail grocery trade in Canada is an uncooked dressing with a preservative of oil to 65 per cent. Salad oil is not necessarily that. It can come in two classes, one with 35 per cent of oil and the other is a cooked dressing. As the hon. member very well knows, some people put out salad dressing under a peculiar name as a low-priced product. You can put out salad dressing in this country at 25 cents for an 8-ounce jar and market it very well under any peculiar or particular name, and some unscrupulous manufacturers are doing just that. They are trying to kid the public into thinking that they are buying a quality article at a cheaper price.
The department is absolutely correct in laying down these regulations. When you market mayonnaise in Canada you say to the public that you are putting a distinct amount of good oil in that mayonnaise. In selling salad dressing you do not. You may say to the public that you are selling this salad dressing under a particular name and the ingredients may be on the label, but I would rather think that very few women buying salad dressing in this country read the small print. I have sold many millions of jars of salad dressing and mayonnaise in my time
Food and Drugs Act
and I would doubt whether 1 per cent of the women who buy it know what is on the label-other than the large print.
The hon. member is entitled to present her views in this house, as I am, but I would ask her to reconsider the matter of the department telling the manufacturer to take an article off the market. I would be in agreement because in British Columbia where it has happened many times it has been for the good of the grocery trade.

I cannot agree. In the first place the hon. member says that salad dressing is a cooked dressing, yet the regulations of the department call for 35 per cent vegetable oil. I do not know how he can reconcile that. It means that no one can put salad dressing on the market unless it has 35 per cent vegetable oil. This label says "oilless mayonnaisfe". I disagree, and I am not talking as a representative of the grocery association; I am talking as a woman and as a cook, and I know what I am talking about. We have been calling this type of thing mayonnaise for a good many years.

May I correct the hon. member? I did not say that all salad dressing had oil in it nor that it was all cooked. I said that there were two qualities of salad dressing as you will see if you read Hansard tomorrow. I should take into consideration the experience my hon. friend has had? but she must remember that there are others in the house who have had just as much experience.

I am not getting into this
discussion about cooks. I want to discuss another matter which is equally important, I believe, to those who are not cooks. It is the question of rum or the description of rum.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member know something about that?

I have had experience. In
the days prior to the time when Newfoundland joined this great nation-when rum was rum, I may say-we had a fine rum known as navy rum and it was sold under a trade name. On the bottle there used to appear the words "approved by the faculty". I never did find out who the faculty actually were. It also said that it was good for the prevention of chills and that it aided the circulation of the blood. Actually, I think it did both. Would the minister say whether or not that would be misleading advertising? There is another rum that we also have had misleadingly described by our friends of the United States forces as screech. I do not know whether that would be misleading advertising or not. I do not even know

Food and Drugs Act
whether the minister is competent to pass an opinion in these matters.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
With regard to the latter, I am certainly not competent. I think that is well known. I think, however, we must maintain a little sense of humour in these matters. There is a difference between that kind of representation and the representation when it is seeking to sell something that it is not. The best example of the value of section 5 is this. The committee will remember that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised with me about a year and a half ago the question of whole-wheat bread. The fact that whole-wheat bread was being advertised but which in fact, in many instances, was not whole-wheat bread, was not necessarily injurious to health but it was deception and people were buying bread thinking that in fact they were getting whole-wheat bread but in a great many instances they were not. Our regulations have been changed, and now no one can advertise whole-wheat bread unless it is in accordance with the prescribed standard and contains a certain percentage of whole-wheat flour.
That principle applies throughout the measure. I was myself one of the victims of this constant use of whole-wheat bread. I was eating whole-wheat bread thinking that as a .result of doing so I was eating less of carbohydrates, only to find out that I was eating the same kind of bread with a different colour. Now it is not possible for that to happen under these regulations.
With regard to the case mentioned by the hon. member for Hamilton West, I can only say this. Mayonnaise does have, in the dictionary meaning, a definite standard. Any English dictionary will show that there has to be a certain amount of vegetable oil, and it has to be a substantial amount. It is not mayonnaise unless oil is in it. That is in the very nature of the product. To advertise mayonnaise as oilless is to advertise something that is not mayonnaise and to give to the public the impression that they are buying in fact mayonnaise. This particular problem did confront us. As my hon. friend knows,
I went into the thing carefully and I did once think that perhaps we were being needlessly strict. We called together in Ottawa representatives of the Canadian Association of Consumers. Mrs. Walton came down here and there were two other ladies from Ottawa who came in to the department, listened to the representations on both sides that were then made, and they agreed with the stand that we were taking.
Is the minister sure of that? I understand that Mrs. Walton was not here.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mrs. Walton was here, and Mrs. Kent and Mrs. Weir, representing the association, and they fully agreed with the stand taken.
That is not the information I got over the telephone.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am giving that information now.

They told me they
definitely wanted oilless dressing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
How did we arrive at this standard? This was not a standard arbitrarily imposed. It was the trade itself which came to us in the first instance in 1936. We sat down with all of the people who were manufacturing mayonnaise and they all agreed that there had to be a prescribed standard in order to avoid misconceptions and deceptions that were being perpetrated, and we arrived at this one; and now the prescribed standard is that 65 per cent of oil must be used. That is the standard. As a result of that we feel that the public now, when they come to buy mayonnaise, will be in fact getting mayonnaise which in its very initial etymological meaning means the use of a substantial amount of oil. I cannot profess to be at all an authority on cooking.
I do not know anything about cooking except that in my heyday I knew something about the value of good cooking. I knew whether food was good or not.
I have before me a cook-book that my wife gave me this morning and I looked up mayonnaise. Here is what mayonnaise is:
This is a thick uncooked emulsion of edible vegetable oil, egg yolk or whole egg, vinegar or lemon Juice, or both, seasoned with salt and other seasonings that are commonly used in its manufacture. It contains at least 50 per cent of edible vegetable oil. The oil content of the average high-grade mayonnaise is about 65 per cent, while the egg content ranges from 5 to 15 per cent.
The technical books all indicate that. Webster's dictionary, which I looked at this morning, indicates that there must be a substantial amount of vegetable oil. However, the particular case that my hon. friend has raised so ably this morning is one that is based on regulation. We feel that our contention is sound. I should be happy at any time to discuss the matter further with my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, it is true that the trade was consulted back in 1936.
I draw to the minister's attention the fact that that was 17 years ago, and a great many of the people who were making mayonnaise at

that time are no longer making it today. A great many of the people who were making mayonnaise without oil at that time have since gone out of the market. Today, as far as I know, this is the only product in Canada which is marketed under that term "oilless mayonnaise". You can bring in all the dictionaries in the country and out of the country, but when a term has popular acceptance as meaning a certain thing, I cannot understand why it should not be allowed. The minister knows right well that in a few years the dictionaries even may have a different definition of that particular term. That has happened before and it may happen again. It seems to me wrong that there should be notice of a regulation back as far as 1936, that nothing is done for 15 or 16 years, and then all of a sudden they dump it in the lap of the one remaining manufacturer in that field. It is discrimination of the highest order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

Mr. Chairman, I was interested in what the minister had to say with respect to the question of brown bread. As he indicated, this matter was raised in the house a number of times, starting back about two years ago. I pointed out to him frequently that deception was being practised. I am glad to know that the regulations which are made under this section were changed a short while ago so far as the labelling of whole-wheat bread is concerned. I think it is also good that the trade has gone in for vitamin enriched white bread. I personally still think that it is not as good as wholewheat bread, but maybe that is a matter of taste. In any event, in a country like Canada where wheat is one of our most important products it does seem to be a shame that so many of our people, in the bread that they eat, should not get the full value that is in the wheat itself.
However, this is the question I want to put to the minister, even under the revised regulations. He seems to be quite satisfied that there can now be no deception. I recognize that is the case where brown bread is wrapped and labelled. But what about the case of unwrapped, unlabelled brown bread? Most people, when they buy a loaf of brown bread -whether it is wrapped and labelled or not- assume that they are getting whole-wheat bread. My point in raising this matter a couple of years ago-and repeatedly during the last two years-was that unwrapped, unlabelled brown bread could be, and was in some cases, simply white bread dyed brown. Has any change been
Food and Drugs Act
made in the regulations so as to require that any bread that is brown must have in it a certain percentage of whole-wheat flour?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Well, one of the reasons of course is that we have our inspection service, which has to deal with the things that cannot be dealt with by regulation, and we are following that aspect of it very closely. speechtext: I take it from what the minister has said that the matter has not been completely cleared up yet. I take it it is still possible for certain firms to put on the market-

speechtext: I think the public should feel that they are getting the fullest protection that it is possible to give them. I would not want to give any other impression.
Are the margarine manufacturers going to be entitled to use the words "pasture sweet"?	.

I have one question in connection with the struggle that the minister has had with whole wheat bread. Do I understand that when the manufacturer of whole wheat bread puts a wrapper on his loaf and advertises it as whole wheat bread the actual wheat germ is in the flour?

There are two points that I should like to bring to the attention of the

Food and Drugs Act
minister. I believe the essence of this offence is sale in Canada. Does the minister feel that it might be advisable to include the word "export" as well as "import"? I think it would be necessary; otherwise you would be selling products that you would not want to go out of Canada.

speechtext: This point arises in another section. speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, to increase the appropriation provided by section 7 for loans under part I from $300,000,000 to $500,000,000, and the appropriation provided by section 13 for loans under part II from $150,000,000 to $250,000,000, also with respect to grants in aid of slum clearance and to certain other matters deemed necessary for the proper administration of the act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before the house seeks authority for the government to introduce certain amendments to the National Housing Act. I will at this stage confine my remarks to the subject matter of the resolution.
When the present National Housing Act was passed in 1944, $100 million was authorized for home ownership loans under part I and to take care of possible losses under the previous housing acts of 1935 and 1938. In 1949 this amount was increased to $300 million. It is now proposed further to increase this appropriation by $200 million, making a total cumulative statutory vote of $500 million for home ownership loans under part I of the act.
For rental housing under part II of the act the original appropriation was $50 million. This was increased to $150 million in 1945. It is now proposed to increase this appropriation by $100 million to $250 million, making a total cumulative statutory vote of $250 million for rental housing loans under part II of the act.
Since 1945 over $1 billion of loans have been approved under the National Housing Act for residential construction in Canada. Of this amount the share of the federal government, including loans made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on direct account, is $379 million.
The reason for asking for increased appropriations at this time is that, of the $300 million appropriated for part I loans, $285 million has been committed, including the amount held to the credit of lending institutions under the pool guarantee arrangement. As hon.

National Housing Act
members know, when a loan is made jointly with a lending institution under the act a certain amount is credited by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to an account held by the corporation in the name of that lending company. This account is for the purpose of making provision for losses that the company may in the future sustain in respect of its share of joint loans. Commitments for rental housing loans under part II, including that credited to the pool guarantee account, approximate $126 million. The balances remaining would not be sufficient to carry the operations of the act through the year 1953.
During the last session the standing committee on banking and commerce examined the annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which administers the National Housing Act. That committee, after its deliberations, recommended that the slum clearance provisions of the National Housing Act be amended. It is now proposed to broaden section 12-the slum clearance section -to provide that the slum area when cleared may be developed under section 35 of the act as a federal-provincial housing project. Under the present legislation the area may be developed by a limited-dividend company, as provided by section 9 of the act, or a life insurance company operating under section 11 of the act. The amendment will further provide for the development of a housing project on an alternative area to be provided by the municipality. This alternative area may be developed by a limited-dividend company, a life company or as a federal-provincial project. There is a condition imposed in the proposed amendment, to the effect that the cleared area must be used for a municipal, provincial or federal public purpose. In other words, the provision relating to the use of an alternative area will apply only if the slum area is designated on the master plan of the municipality for public use. The committee recommended also that the cleared area might be used for commercial or other purposes. It is considered that if land is to be acquired and cleared for commercial or industrial uses the responsibility for its acquisition and clearance should rest with the commercial or industrial interests concerned, and authority to make the cleared land thus available is not being sought in the proposed amendments.
Other amendments contained in the proposed legislation are of a procedural or technical nature. I will at this time refer briefly to them.
It is proposed to include a clause in the act that will remove any doubt that lending companies operating under the act have the

corporate power to make and administer loans on an agency basis on behalf of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The government is by the proposed amendments also seeking authority for the corporation to make supplementary advances in connection with existing loans which it has made on its own account. This will allow the corporation to advance borrowers' charges where it becomes necessary to do so. At the present time the corporation has this power jointly with a lending institution in respect of a joint loan, but it does not have the same authority with respect to direct loans.
The section under which the integrated housing plan was operated and under which the arrangement in respect of defence workers has been made is being amended. The proposed amendments will require that a builder pay a premium for the undertaking of the corporation to purchase from him any house that he is unable to sell on the market. The section is also being amended with reference to the class of persons to whom a builder must first offer a house for sale. The present provisions refer to veterans. It is proposed to add specifically defence workers.
Finally, an amendment is proposed regarding rental insurance. As hon. members know, there is a three-year rental control on projects financed under the rental insurance plan. This control is imposed by the builder in his agreement with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Pursuant to the present legislation, such three-year period runs from the completion of the whole project. This imposes a hardship on builders of large projects where upwards of a year may elapse between the renting of the first units and the final completion of the project. The proposed amendment will have the three-year period running from the completion of each unit or group of units.

Mr. Chairman, this, rather strangely, is the first time in the course of the entire present session of parliament that there has been a debate on housing. We have been in session since November 20, 1952, yet this is the first occasion on which housing has been the subject of a debate in the house. There were some comments on it during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and on the budget, but apart from that housing has not been the subject of debate during this session.
This is a resolution looking to the introduction, as I gather from the minister's statement, of what will be a rather extensive bill amending the housing act. It is not my purpose this morning to discuss at any length the contents of the minister's state-

ment nor the type of amendment that he has indicated. On the motion for second reading, when we have the contents of the bill before us, we shall have a much more suitable opportunity for that discussion.
I intend this morning to content myself with some brief observations concerning the housing problem in general. This problem has not receded in importance; it is still a prime problem facing all of Canada. On the last occasion when we had a debate on this subject in the house, on July 3, 1952, I reviewed the evidence that had been given before the committee on banking and commerce in the 1952 session. At its meetings during that year the committee had made an extensive inquiry into housing and the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I summed up the evidence which had been given to the committee, for the years 1946-1951 inclusive, as will be found on page 4176 of Hansard of July 3, 1952, as follows: For the six-year period the totals are these:	net family formations,
513,000; new housing units completed 495,887.
That means that in the six-year period we had not even kept abreast of new housing needs, let alone make any reduction in the very substantial backlog of housing needs which existed at the conclusion of the war. In other words, house construction in Canada had fallen behind current family formations in the same period to the extent of 17,113 units.
We have had no authoritative estimate of the extent of the housing shortage in Canada. Mr. Mansur, president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, stated before the banking and commerce committee a year ago that he was not prepared to commit himself to any estimate on that subject. He did indicate that he had reservations concerning the estimate of housing shortage by the Curtis commission in 1944, but he himself was not prepared to commit himself to any estimate in that regard.
Whatever may be the best estimate, the fact is that there is still a great and pressing backlog of housing need in Canada. I have said "housing need" because there seems to be something of a change in emphasis as between housing need and housing demand. Housing need is not to be measured simply in terms of effective housing demand. When we speak of effective housing demand we are speaking in terms of economic demand on the part of those who have the means to satisfy their need if houses were available.
Of the various factors which over the post-war period have been responsible for
National Housing Act
retarding house construction, these have been mentioned from time to time: shortage of labour, shortage of materials, high prices, shortage of mortgage funds, shortage of serviced land and others. Under present-day conditions there has been a change of responsibility as between those different factors. Today it cannot be said that a shortage of labour is responsible for any retardation of house construction in Canada. As a matter of fact, while the minister has not given figures on expected house construction as estimated for this year, as I followed his statement, the figure that will be attained this year, according to estimates of officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, will be substantially below the capacity of the Canadian construction industry which competent officials of that industry have claimed, namely, a total of 130,000 housing units. Whether that figure be accepted, or some figure closely approximating it, the fact of the matter is that it is abundantly clear that the capacity of the Canadian construction industry is very substantially in excess of the rate of construction of houses.
The next factor deserving of comment is the supply of materials. Happily we are no longer faced with a shortage of materials; no longer can a shortage of materials be regarded as a factor delaying house construction. In a recent publication of the Department of Trade and Commerce entitled "Supply of Building Materials in Canada. Outlook 1953" we have a review of the 1952 position and a sketch of the outlook for 1953. The 1952 position is summed up in these words:
The supply of building materials in relation to requirements was better in 1952 than in any previous post-war year, and such shortages as did exist did not affect to any great extent the overall volume of construction achieved. Even so, with construction at an all-time high, a few strategic materials remained very scarce and a number of small projects for which supplies had not been obtained in advance were delayed. At the same time the decline of house building activity during the first six months of the year brought on a sharp drop in demand for a wide range of materials, forcing manufacturers to cut back production.
Then the publication proceeds to comment upon the extent to which shortages appeared during the year in cement and heavy structural steel beams, and it continues:
Despite these shortages, 1952 saw a fairly general movement of building materials into good supply. In fact, for the first time since the war, the production of a large number of building materials was cut back early in the year due to reduced demand and to temporarily inflated inventories. Thus, of the materials covered in this report, the production of 20 declined while the production of only 12 increased. Moreover, some of the shortages which appeared following the upswing in house building were due more to the fact that

National Housing Act
stocks had been unduly depleted by mid-year than to insufficiency of productive capacity.
That is its review with respect to building materials during 1952. What of the outlook for 1953? This publication sums it up in these words:
The outlook for the supply of building materials in 1953 is distinctly favourable. While the volume of construction is expected to be even larger than in 1952, its composition will be more balanced from the standpoint of the Canadian building materials industries.
That is an encouraging outlook with respect to building materials.
Commenting on prices in a recent speech to the house builders' association in Toronto on March 24, Mr. Mansur said that in 1952 the prices of houses were relatively stable. It is a happy circumstance if the cost of housing has ceased its upward climb. Whether that proves to be too optimistic an estimate we shall not be long in learning. Nevertheless it is, if this statement is justified, a hopeful augury that at least we have achieved stability in house building costs. The fact remains, however, that house building costs are extremely high, and in all fairness this is the factor which has created that difference that I mentioned earlier between housing need and effective economic housing demand, because unquestionably if the cost of construction of houses were lower they would be within the economic reach of many more people than can purchase them today.
Now, sir, I should like to say a word about mortgage funds. The minister did not make any comment on this subject in his statement. He asserted several days ago, in reply to a question, that there was no justification for the charge that in one particular municipality there had been a strike on the part of the lending institutions. In fairness, Mr. Chairman, it is a fact that must be recognized that there has been very general co-operation on the part of the lending institutions with respect to the policy that parliament has approved and which is written in the terms of part I of the National Housing Act. It is a fact that many people have not been able to obtain loans to the extent that or in the localities where they desired them, and for that reason some have sought to criticize the lending institutions. The fact of the matter is that in this country today the financial resources of the lending institutions are being used to their limit in assisting house construction under part I of the National Housing Act.
Because of the rise in the cost of house construction, the investment of the same amount of money today in loans under part I of the National Housing Act does not provide as many loans as was the case two [Mr. Fleming.!
years ago or even one year ago. The fact of the matter is that the average amount of mortgage money committed per loan is higher than it has been previously. Therefore the same total of investment through part I of the National Housing Act on the part of the lending institutions has not made available as many mortgage loans even though the total of money so made available is as large as and actually larger than in the previous year.
The present system under part I has many satisfactory features about it. On the other hand, there are unquestionably very great strains today upon the resources available for house construction through part I of the National Housing Act. One is the physical limit that exists on the resources of the lending institutions available for lending on mortgage security. Others take the form, and naturally, of a selective approach on the part of the lending institutions. We will look with interest for a report from the minister on the extent to which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has itself attempted to step into the breach in the case of municipalities up to 50,000 population where adequate mortgage loans from lending institutions have not been available under part I of the National Housing Act.
I should like to draw attention to this fact, and I think it is a fact that either is not generally known or is not generally appreciated. When the lending institutions under part I of the act are called upon to provide a loan it means a tremendous amount of detail work on their part. I am told that there are no fewer than 45 pieces of paper that have to be handled in placing every loan by one of these lending institutions under part I, and these 45 pieces of paper do not include the mortgage itself. Therefore it is not unnatural that the lending institutions, faced with a load of administrative work of that kind, are seeking to reduce the work that is thrown upon them in that regard, and it is not unnatural that their approach should become selective in this field in the face of a very great demand. I should like to hear some statement from the minister as to the policy that the government proposes to offer in the face of that admitted problem.
I come now to a brief statement of what is today unquestionably the most serious and difficult of all the problems contributing to the retardation of house construction in Canada. I refer to the shortage of serviced land. The great need for housing today is in our urban areas, and the acceleration of the program of defence production has contributed greatly to the sharpening of the need of more homes in the large urban areas,

particularly those industrial centres where defence production has been a noticeable factor in the local economy. It has reached a point where indeed, Mr. Chairman, some municipalities are so overwhelmed with the burden of providing services for land that they are doing what is within their power to discourage house construction within their municipal borders. In some cases this takes the form of requiring the builder or subdivider of land to pay in advance the costs of installing all services. The burden on our municipalities today, particularly on fast growing urban municipalities or those suburban municipalities that surround the great metropolitan centres, is very great.
They are still working under the handicap of a very limited tax base, a tax base which has remained virtually unchanged since 1867, a tax base that is utterly inadequate to enable municipalities to cope effectively today with the problem which has in part at least been left on their doorsteps by senior governments. If we wish to make an effective contribution to meeting the housing problem in Canada today we will need to do something effective to assist municipalities. I tried to sum it up in these words in the last housing debate on July 3, 1952, as found at page 4178 of Hansard:
If we want to help the housing problem in Canada, we cannot have a better slogan than this: Help the municipal governments!
We are not helping the municipal governments enough under the terms of this legislation. The minister has indicated that there are going to be some amendments with respect to section 35 of the act. The extent to which they are going to bring any help at all to municipalities was not clear from his statement, and I am not going to comment upon that subject until we see the text of the bill. It may well be that in some respects the effect is going to be to increase the burdens on municipalities, but I shall not attempt to venture comment on that subject until I see the bill. But the fact remains that the municipalities today, particularly the fast growing metropolitan and suburban municipalities surrounding industrial centres, are simply not financially able to cope with the housing problems that are being thrust upon them. And what is needed today, as imperatively as ever in this country's history, is a dominion-provincial conference to work out an understanding with respect to taxation sources which will assure to the municipalities sources of revenue in this respect that will assist them adequately to meet whatever share of the burden of the housing problem may be left to them to discharge.
Sir, slum clearance is a problem of great importance. Progress has lagged lamentably
National Housing Act
in this respect. Hopes that were held out in this house in 1949 when section 35 of the act was enacted have been disappointed. Much needs to be done in this respect. It is difficult of course to make the scheme of section 35 work when it requires co-operation with respect to each project on the part of the three levels of government involved. In that respect the section is cumbersome in its operation and I hope that the amendments to section 35 that are to appear in the bill will hold out some measure of hope that some of the difficulties which now surround the operation of section 35 will be met and removed. There certainly must be a more effective marrying of sections 12 and 35. I know it is a matter that the minister has had under study since the committee on banking and commerce made its recommendations on this point a year ago. I look for effective amendment in this respect when the bill is introduced.
There are just two other matters, Mr. Chairman, which I shall mention briefly in closing. There is one subject which has not been adequately examined in this house or justified. It relates to expenditure of a kind which is not of itself calculated to assist the housing problem in this country very much. On December 17, 1952, at page 820 of Hansard the minister brought in answers to certain questions asked by the hon. member for Wentworth concerning the cost of construction of the handsome new head office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Let me say at once that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has itself to be housed adequately. It has to carry on very important business and I should be the last one to say that it should not be properly accommodated. However, Mr. Speaker, in times like these when the levels of government that are greatly concerned with the provision of municipal services for housing are faced with very great difficulties, and when the provision that has been made by the federal government to assist in meeting the housing problem has not always been generous, I ask, Mr. Chairman, if the taxpayers of this country will regard it as justifiable that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have constructed in this building-

The project consists of 428 homes, all of which are occupied and are either owned or rented by ex-servicemen. They are married ex-servicemen in all cases. Those houses have been occupied by the residents for periods of up to seven years.
When they were first constructed they were all rented and then, in keeping with the general policy, the corporation in 1951 offered those homes for sale to the tenants and a number of the tenants purchased.

A number of the veterans who purchased their houses from the corporation, as I have

National Housing Act
indicated, about 160 of them, continue to pay rent. On March 30 of this year, while still paying rent, they received a notice from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which I think is not a model notice to be followed by landlords in such cases. On the contrary, it seems to me to be couched in very harsh terms as applied to these veterans who have obviously been satisfactory tenants. The notice is signed for the corporation by F. J. Melvin, administrator. It is dated March 30, 1953, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
We hereby give you notice to quit and deliver up to this corporation on the 30th day of April next, quiet possession of the premises situated at now held by you as our tenant.
We offer to lease to you these same premises at a monthly rental of $	commencing on
the first day of May 1953.
Included in your present rental payment for the house you occupy is an amount of $84.84 per annum which is turned over to the municipality as payment in lieu of taxes. In accordance with a request from the corporation of the city of Ottawa, we have now agreed to collect full taxes from the houses remaining unsold in these projects and this necessitates the new rental stated above. This, we think, is only fair since those persons thrifty enough to purchase their homes earlier have of course been liable to full taxes from the date of purchase.
A new lease, at the new rental, will be ready for your signature at our office any time after May 1, 1953.
If the corporation is now under legal obligation to pay the city of Ottawa the full taxes on these properties, and they are no longer covered by the kind of agreement under which first of all Wartime Housing Limited and later Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation were making payments to the municipalities in lieu of taxes and at a rate usually lower than taxes, whatever they may be, and whatever considerations ought to arise out of that, it seems to me that is a very harsh way to proceed. I should like to ask the minister, as the minister responsible for the administration of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, whether instead of taking this harsh course he does not think that this is a matter to be proceeded with on the basis of conference and an attempt to bring together those 160 veteran tenants.
They resent, and quite naturally, the suggestion that they were not thrifty because they did not purchase their homes. I think the minister will agree that is a very invidious sort of comparison to put in a letter of this kind. A notice to vacate or a notice to treat for a hew lease or new rent is one thing, but to suggest to the recipients that they have not been thrifty is I think an insult to many of them. As a matter of fact, many of them have not bought because they were not in a position to do so. There is this further fact.

I am told that many of them say that they were orally assured by officials of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation at the time when the tenants were invited to purchase their homes that whatever they paid by way of rent would be taken into account in establishing the price in the event of purchase. They are now told that the corporation does not acknowledge that in the case of those who did not buy at that time; that no right arises in their behalf in consequence of having paid rent.
I say to the minister with respect that that is something he should look into and make sure that justice is going to be done to these veterans. Certainly there is no occasion for giving summary notice to a group of worthy veterans, 160 in number, who have obviously been very satisfactory tenants. Therefore if the tax position is changed, if it is costing the corporation more to carry these properties, then that of course must be taken into account, but it is not a justification for treating these veterans harshly and summarily in the tone of this letter.
I bring that matter to the minister's attention and ask him to delay proceedings of this kind and to negotiate with these veterans and find a better way of meeting the problem than is indicated in the way it has been handled heretofore.
In conclusion may I ask the minister for a fuller statement of policy than he gave the house this morning. The house and the country are entitled to know what proposals the government has to make to the house for making more progress in meeting the housing problem than is being made at the present time. Whatever may be said of these amendments-and there will be fuller opportunity to discuss them when the bill is before the house-the house is entitled to some clear statement of policy that will indicate that something more effective is going to be done than is being done at the present time.

I make no apologies for speaking at some length on this resolution. Housing is still one of Canada's most baffling social problems. This resolution has been on the order paper since December 5, and I submit that if the government had assigned to it the place and time that its seriousness merits it would have been called earlier. It would not have been hurried through parliament in the last week or two of a parliamentary session. It would have been passed on to a committee where ample opportunity would have been given for the study of this very serious problem.
With the single exception of national defence there is no subject today of any more

vital importance to great numbers of Canadian people than is that of housing. Every year since I came to parliament we have had a debate on this subject. In session after session hon. members on this side of the house, as well as hon. members on the other side, have put forward suggestions to the government as to how this problem could best be met. But we have gone on year after year without being any closer to reaching a solution than we were some years ago.
The amendments which will be introduced as a result of the legislation before us may help, in so far as they make more federal funds available. To that extent the measure will help the situation. But I submit that although for years Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been trying to work with private lending organizations, with real estate boards, with associations of speculative builders and with provincial governments, it has not yet reached any solution to our housing problem. The situation today is as bad as it was at the end of the war.
There are no official figures as to just what the need is; but officials have estimated that today in Canada we need anywhere from
600,000	to 700,000 homes. The 500,000 which have been built since the war have not provided for the new families created in that time. The backlog has increased, and under today's policy nothing is being done to catch up with that backlog.
Housing is something more than just the process of obtaining places in which to live. As I have said, it is a social problem. In a special issue on housing dated December 15, 1952, the Canadian Welfare Council has much to say about the effects of poor housing upon our community life. In part the article states:
It has become well known from studies made in large and small cities that the rates of juvenile delinquency, disease, retardation and other difficulties at school, serious home accidents and fires, are higher in neighbourhoods of poor and overcrowded housing than in others.
Newark, New Jersey, has made a study, published under the title "Social Effects of Public Housing" in which the following conclusions are reached:
The disease, accident and juvenile delinquency rates, which could be measured exactly, were better among the re-housed groups than among the control groups. In the things which could not be measured exactly, and in which the re-housed group could not be compared statistically with the control group, the study had to rely on reports from the mothers: The majority of the mothers said their children had improved in their school work, were easier to keep clean, had better places to play; that their families were happier, and had been able to save money or purchase equipment for their homes. One hundred per cent reported no fires or serious home accidents.
