That report goes on to look at the other side of the picture, housing as a social problem.
What is the other side of the picture? When housing is poor, health suffers, there is friction among members of families; budgets are thrown out of gear, families are often separated, social agencies find that they are frustrated in their efforts to help, children cannot play properly, new Canadians get fed up, and the costs of health and welfare services are too high.
And then are set out page after page of details from investigations held in Montreal, Hamilton, Toronto, Halifax and other Canadian cities, pointing out the disastrous effect upon society of bad housing conditions.
I believe the trouble with our housing policy under this government is that the government has placed the cart before the horse. In its anxiety to bolster private enterprise the government has placed the interests of lending institutions before the interests of the community at large. As a result we are not getting housing at a price that the majority of Canadians can afford, either to purchase or to rent. We must recognize that housing is a social problem, and that the provision of government assistance in housing for people who cannot afford either to buy or to rent accommodation is no more socialistic than the provision of hospitals, schools and pure water on a community basis.
I think we must change our entire point of view in connection with this whole business of government assistance in housing. This is not a field that should be left free for private enterprise to exploit. It is of far too great importance in the life of the community to be left to exploitation for profit by private enterprise. It is one field in which the government is justified in giving a public service through the provision of homes at prices people can afford to pay.
_ The social cost involved in government subsidies for low-rental housing, or the cost which would be involved in a government policy which would make loans at a much lower rate of interest than offered by the private lending companies, would be more than offset by the savings that would be effected in other services communities are called upon to give, by reason of the fact that there are poor and overcrowded housing conditions.
Let us look at the results of the government's housing policy to date, so that we may realize just how far short of providing a solution this resolution falls. Since 1950 there -has been a decline in the actual number of houses being built. I submit that a successful government policy, a realistic policy designed to meet the needs of the people instead of the interests of the lending

National Housing Act
institutions, would be a policy that year after year would bring about an increase in the number of houses being built.
The second indisputable fact is that the backlog of housing which existed at the end of the war has increased. We have not been able to close the gap between the need which existed at the end of the war and the supply. As a matter of fact, we have not been able to provide enough houses to house the new families of Canada.
The third fact that must be recognized is that as a result of the present government policy the cost of houses today places them beyond the means of most Canadian people. We have it on the authority of Mr. Mansur that only those with incomes of $3,500 a year or more can avail themselves of the benefits offered under the National Housing Act, that only those with incomes of $3,500 and more have sufficient income to meet the carrying charges on some of the cheapest houses, those costing in the neighbourhood of $10,000 which is the cheapest house being built under the National Housing Act.
The fourth fact which I think we must recognize is that there is a desperate shortage of rental housing. Mr. Mansur again tells us that $85 per month is the lowest economic Tent that can be charged for a 4-roomed fully serviced dwelling house. Eighty-five *dollars a month is just more than the average workingman can afford to pay today. Any housing policy that is designed to meet the needs of the people of this country will make some provision for rental housing because we are told on good authority that at least one-third of the people of Canada cannot buy or expect to pay for homes.
I know that section 35 of the housing act provides for rental projects being undertaken in co-operation with the provincial and municipal governments, but for some reason these projects are not making very much headway. They are not meeting the needs of the people. They are not meeting the situation. The government says that the initiative must be taken by the local municipality. Surely there is a place here for more dynamic leadership on the part of the federal housing authorities. Surely there is room here for the federal housing authority taking steps to encourage municipalities to get into this field in cooperation with the provincial and federal governments so that low rental housing may be provided.
Next, we have not as yet had any comprehensive planning on a community basis. What work the government's housing authority has done has been on a piecemeal basis. It has been project by project, street by street, and a bit here and there to relieve the direct

conditions. There has not yet been evolved by the government or the housing authority any comprehensive housing plan on a community basis to meet this problem.
There is another aspect of this matter which is sometimes lost sight of. Over the last few years tens of thousands of Canadians have bought homes and assumed mortgages. Should we have a business recession, should there come some unemployment or reduction in wages, these people will lose the homes they have acquired and into which they have put their savings, just as surely as they lost them by the thousand in the early thirties.
This is not an impossible situation. Only a few days ago when the first news of a possible peace came there was a slump on the New York stock exchange which indicated how sensitive modern business is to present conditions. As a matter of fact there are those who wonder whether we can afford peace and maintain prosperity under our present economic system. People by the thousand have assumed mortgages over the past few years on houses costing $10,000, $11,000 and $12,000 which they will be able to hold only so long as we maintain prosperity, full employment and high wage levels.
I submit that the present situation with regard to housing is all the positive proof that is required that some radical changes in the government's policy with regard to housing is necessary. The present policy, whereby the federal government agency, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, enters into contracts with private lending institutions to make loans available to builders, has not proved to be a workable solution to our housing problem. That approach to the problem may be good for the lending institution but it is not getting homes built at prices at which most Canadians can afford to buy or rent. I submit that the supreme test of any housing policy is not its financial benefits to the private lending institutions, it is whether or not it gets houses built at prices at which people can afford to buy or rent. Judged by that standard the government's policy in connection with housing since the war has failed, and failed miserably.
Interest rates on loans are one of the most important factors in carrying charges on homes. We hear a great deal about the increased cost of labour, the increased cost of materials and so on, but we hear little about interest charges. Mr. Nathan Strauss in "Seven Myths of Housing" tells us that a reduction in financial charges, interest and amortization by one-half would effect a greater reduction in annual cost than cutting

in half the cost of both material and labour. The reduction by one-half of interest and amortization charges would reduce the overall cost of a house more than it would be reduced by a one-half reduction in the cost of both material and labour.
Catherine Baur, another housing authority, tells us in the International Labour Review of July, 1945, and she gives a statistical table to support her statement, that a reduction of 2 per cent in interest rates will mean a bigger saving in the total cost than a 20 per cent reduction in the cost of the structure itself. In my opinion it is not reasonable to expect the private lending institutions to lend their money for housing projects at interest rates which would bring the cost of these houses within the reach of those who need them. I submit that is the function of government. The private loan companies exist for the express purpose of making a fair return on their investment for the benefit of their shareholders. There is no one criticizing them for doing that. It is not their function to provide a social service to the community. I submit that is the function of government.
Another drawback to the government's policy on housing, in addition to the high interest rate which is required by reason of the government's policy, is the burden which is thrown on the municipalities. Mr. Mansur has told us that one of the great drawbacks is the lack of serviced lands. The municipalities are loath to provide serviced land, to provide school facilities and so on for the new communities where large housing projects are undertaken. It has been estimated that, under such circumstances, a municipality is called upon to be responsible for about $2,000 per home through the provision of serviced land, various other services, school accommodation, and so on. Today, the municipalities are loath to undertake that responsibility. That is one aspect of the housing problem which this government's policy fails to meet entirely.
In order to help the drastic housing problem, I want to place on the record a few suggestions advocated by the C.C.F., suggestions that have been approved by our national organization and which may be considered as official C.C.F. policy on the matter of housing. I shall outline these briefly and comment on them later. In our opinion a policy that is to meet the needs of the Canadian people regarding housing must, first of all, provide a reduction in interest rates to 2 per cent by having Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation solely responsible for the issuing of these loans. We recom-
National Housing Act
mend that the federal government should set up a special fund1 for this purpose, and that money from this fund should be available not only in the industrial centres in which lending institutions now lend money, but in the small communities and farming districts where private lending institutions will not lend money at all for these purposes.
Secondly, we suggest that there be an increase in loans from 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the lending value of the housing project. Third, we recommend an increase in the amortization period. Most of the current loans now run for twenty years. There have been some forward steps taken recently whereby the period has been increased to twenty-five years. We recognize that good housing authorities now maintain that that amortization period should be extended to thirty or thirty-five years in the case of houses of brick or similar construction.
The fourth suggestion is the inauguration of rental subsidy funds on condition that only municipalities or public housing authorities should receive the subsidy. Such a subsidy would be granted on condition that the municipality or recipient would comply with the requirements of a comprehensive housing program. This subsidy would permit a sharp reduction in the present high rents so that the low income dwellers, who cannot afford to build homes under even the most favourable conditions, would benefit. The fifth point we suggest is that the federal government make grants to the provinces to be turned over to the municipalities for the construction of schools and other public facilities which are presently a heavy expense charged to the municipality when a new housing site comes into being. On this point I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Eglinton when he suggests there should be a conference of federal, provincial and municipal authorities in an effort to work out some plan whereby the federal government will come to the assistance of municipalities in meeting the cost of school construction and the provision of other facilities.
We submit that housing is of sufficient national importance to warrant the federal government faking some action in this connection. Finally, we submit that there should be an increase in the number of scholarships provided under the National Housing Act to train a larger number of badly needed administrators in the housing field. We commend what is being done already in that field. I understand that somewhere between nine and ten scholarships are granted annually. Our suggestion is that the number of scholarships should be increased and that

National Housing Act
more housing administrators should be trained.
We put forth these suggestions on the premise, as I said before, that housing is a social problem. It is not just an economic problem, but it is a social problem of great national importance. It is not simply a matter of finding a place in which people may live. It is a matter which will have a direct bearing upon the lives and upon the happiness of our Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the first occasion upon which I have had the privilege of speaking about housing. I do not think there is a question which is of greater interest to the Canadian people than housing, because nothing gives greater dissatisfaction to the people across this country than living in poor housing accommodation.
On many occasions, Mr. Chairman, I have condemned the type of housing which the government has built in the past. That goes back from the very inception of the national building program. After the war when we started to build wartime houses some of the most terrible structures were built in the name of houses. We come to the veterans' housing, V.L.A., and that too, a government-sponsored affair, was a disgrace across the country. I know that it did provide some shelter for the returned men but I said at the time that it would not be long before that kind of house would be a disgrace to the community in which it was built. Even now you can go through the city of Ottawa, the city of Winnipeg, the city of Calgary or any other large city and you can pick out those V.L.A. houses as far as you can see them. People are somewhat reluctant to buy property in the vicinity of V.L.A. houses because they are eyesores in the community in which they are built.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
They are all right in
Edmonton.
Well, perhaps you had something to do with building them, I do not know-and I do not know whether contracts for them were let out to tender-and that is just a passing reference.
Where are these houses?

I am serious, Mr. Chairman; they are not a good thing for the communities in which they were built. They do serve a purpose, which is shelter, but surely in this day and age we can build more than shelter for our people.
We are mighty proud of them.

It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that our attention is being centred

too greatly on apartments and rooming houses and such like rather than having the main emphasis put upon private homes. I am not overlooking the necessity for having low-rental projects, I think they are necessary; but it seems to me that the greatest effort should be put upon building homes for families. It is not a good thing in my judgment to have a number of families housed in a rooming house project. That is not conducive to the good bringing up of children. There is no adequate place for the children to play and the grounds are not adequate for beautification of the structure after it is built. I think that one of our big mistakes is that we are not paying sufficient attention to home structure for the single family unit.
Again, Mr. Chairman, the housing programs which we are undertaking now are not doing the job they were intended to do. We are not building homes for the people who need them. It is senseless to say that you have to have a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation set-up costing over $80 million a year, and that you have got to have a lending institution to lend money to a man who is drawing $15,000 or $20,000 a year. He can look after his own problems and so can the fellow who is getting $7,000 or $8,000 a year. The people we are concerned with are those who are not in a financial position to have available that kind of money. The minister himself realizes this, for when he was speaking not long ago at the banquet of the Appraisal Institute of Canada, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of Thursday, April 2, 1953, he had this to say -and I wholly agree with him though I am amazed that he is not doing anything about it. It is headed, "Low Rent Aid":
Mr. Winters said that not more than one-third of Canada's families could afford new houses-
I heartily endorse that.
-either to rent or to own. In the past, this had been overcome by families living in houses that were second, third, fourth or even fifth hand.
But if enough new houses weren't found, he stated, it would affect the people at the bottom of the scale-the people who were living in dilapidated and obsolescent housing.
I would not dispute that for a moment. I think it is exactly the case, and those are the people whom the National Housing Act is supposed to be assisting.
What are we doing about it? Not a thing. We cannot use the excuse that there is a shortage of material because all of the builders' organizations in the country, and the department too, have stated on many occasions that there is ample building material in the form of lumber, plumbing equipment and so on. In days gone by, there might have been the excuse of shortage of materials but that condition does not exist today.

I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen of Monday, February 16, 1953, headed: "The Government's Modest Housing Target".
With labour and materials again in good supply, it has become physically possible to start building more homes than at any time since the start of the Korean war. Yet the government's program does not seem over-ambitious. Speaking in Winnipeg, Mr. Winters, the resources minister, said merely that 1953 construction might reach the "high" levels of pre-Korea years. In 1950, 92,000 dwelling units were built. This construction about kept pace with new demand, but did little to reduce the backlog. Since then, home building has fallen. In 1951, only 68,000 new units were started. Last year, the figure was 76,000. Yet the need is greater than ever, for family formation and immigration have continued at a high rate.
So once again the minister says that we are not doing the job as it should be done.
In speaking of materials and how we are keeping our program up with the times the National Housebuilders Association in a circular dated February 25, 1953, gives "Facts and figures for your use in the debate on housing".
House production is dropping. Despite an upward trend in the last half of 1952, production for the year was only 75,000 units, 10,000 less than in 1951 and 17,000 less than in 1950.
Those are dominion bureau of statistics figures.
Our backlog of unbuilt housing is growing. The total is now 490,000 units made up as follows:
