That certainly does not indicate that we are making any progress in this housing field. The minister has pointed out on many occasions, as have others, why the condition exists. There are apparently some obstacles in the way of home building but certainly labour is not one of them, because I remember seeing a report put out not so long ago by the contractors organization where there were something like 40,000 or 50,000 unemployed carpenters looking for jobs. One of the obstacles that have been brought forward is the lack of serviced land which is said to be holding back our building program. I do not think that should be a serious problem, but I will discuss it later on. The second obstacle to home building is the down payment; and the third is the shortage of mortgage money.
Let me speak about the serviced land for a moment and see whether that should offer such a great obstacle to our house building program if it is properly conducted. Here is what was done in the province of Alberta;
National Housing Act
and you will excuse me if I keep referring to the province of Alberta because it is one of the most outstanding provinces. When you are talking about progress you just cannot help referring to it. It was in 1950 that the province of Alberta started what they called a program of self-liquidating projects. Under that program of self-liquidating projects they included such things as water systems for municipalities, electrical supply for municipalities, construction in part of schools and so on. They set up a $5 million revolving fund and they lent that money to the municipalities at 2 per cent. As far as my figures go, up to the present time of that money $460,000 has been paid back and they have not lost a penny of it yet. The fund was established in 1950 and since that time $17 million has been placed in it.
I do not see what better security you could have, under the heading of a self-liquidating project, than a man's home. If a man gets into fairly tough straits, he will even sell his car in order to keep his house intact. He will cut down his standard of living to make his monthly payments on his home. It forms the very basis of security. This year, in 1953, the province of Alberta has budgeted for a little bit over $174 million. Out of that amount there has been set up an additional fund of $25 million to further assist the municipalities. I have heard some talk here this afternoon about the municipalities being overburdened. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that they are overburdened; but I also suggest that the province of Alberta is assisting the municipalities in developing self-liquidating projects at an extremely low rate of interest.
They have oil.

Oil is not the main factor at all. In 1951-and my mind goes back to those figures because they are given by the dominion bureau of statistics-if I remember correctly our total income on oil that year was $121 million. That did not begin to equal the revenue which was obtained from cattle and hogs in the province of Alberta. It is true that oil has been of assistance to us, but it has not been the main factor of our prosperity by any manner of means. Agriculture is by far the leading and basic industry of western Canada and it is the backbone of Canada as well. Let nobody say, "Oh well, it is because you have oil out in Alberta." Certainly oil has helped us, but our plans were laid a long time before oil began to be produced in any large amount.
I think if the provinces were to assist the municipalities, as I have indicated, by setting up a revolving fund for self-liquidating pro-

National Housing Act jects such as sewers, light, roads, schools, streets and water, it would go a long way towards solving that problem of servicing land.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Is that revolving fund still in operation in Alberta?

As far as I know, yes; and they have increased it to $25 million now. That was according to the 1953 program. But the $25 million was an additional aid to the municipalities. If my memory serves me correctly, I think the rate of interest was 2J per cent on that $25 million but 2 per cent on the $5 million. I suggest that the federal government should take a lesson from that example.
God help us.
I beg the hon. member's pardon?
He said "God help us".

My hon. friend was looking for divine aid? Maybe a little bit of it would do them good.
The next obstacle to housing that I mentioned a moment ago was the down payment. That was the big trouble according to the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) when he was speaking to this Appraisal Institute of Canada on April 2. The problem that was in his mind was the fact that we are not doing anything to assist these people who are in the low income brackets, and well it might be, because there is where the difficulty lies. But I do not think as yet he has solved that problem. He might say to me that there are instances where the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is lending money at a cheaper rate in some localities; and I think over there in Hull was one of them, if my memory serves me correctly. But under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans are guaranteed up to 80 per cent of the lending value. That does not mean for a moment that they are financing the construction of that house.
The big question that comes in there is the lending value. For instance, a house might cost $15,000 but the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not value that house at $15,000. They might say that the lending value of that house is only $10,000; and I think that in 90 per cent of the cases that is exactly what they do, because they are making themselves doubly sure when they set the appraisal value of that house. Then they lend up to 80 per cent of that value.


Then the lending institutions come along and charge 51 per cent, for interest on the loans which they make. How can people who are so poor that they cannot afford the down payment on a house pay 51 per cent interest on a loan? It just cannot be done, and the obvious truth is that they are not doing it. Therefore they are not getting homes. The minister can go out to these institutes and preach all he likes, and he can say, "There is where our trouble lies"; but what is he doing about it?
I well recall, Mr. Chairman, just after the war or in the last part of the war, what took place when there was no place for the mortgage companies to lend their money; the farmers were getting out of debt and so were the others. The government came to their aid and put up to them this housing proposition whereby they could lend their money out at a good rate of interest. Then just as soon as other fields become more attractive they cease lending for home building and put their money out on those other projects. I do not think it should be the purpose of a national housing plan to assist financial corporations. If we are going out to build houses, let us build houses and not go into the financial field.
Under N.H.A. a house may cost $11,600. The maximum loan on that house, under the present set-up, would be about $7,906 and the down payment would be $3,154. According to the bureau of statistics, about 75 per cent of the people of Canada earn less than $3,000 a year. Just where is the ordinary man going to get a down payment of $3,154 on a $11,000 home? When he does not even earn that amount in the full year, where is he going to get the money? For us to stand up here and say that this class of society can build homes is just nonsense, when they do not earn that amount for a full year's work.
According to the dominion bureau of statistics, 1951 census report, about 75 per cent of 2 million families earn less than $3,000 a year. Nineteen per cent of these earned between $2,500 and $3,000;	25 per cent
between $2,000 and $2,500; and 22J per cent between $1,000 and $2,000 and 7 per cent of these earned less than $1,000. The number in the last group consists of about 132,000 families. When you find people with incomes within these brackets you ask yourself, just how are they going to get a downpayment of $3,150 to build a house? So far as I know, any plans the government has will not meet that problem.
The next obstacle I mentioned was the shortage of mortgage money. Last year we used about $175 million. This year it is expected we shall use about $225 million.

When it comes to these mortgage companies lending money we find that they are not taking much risk. In the first place, their appraisal value is down below the actual value of the house. In the next place, the government guarantees them 25 per cent loss. What have they got to lose? But yet, according to the public accounts of this year, the government lost $686,837.04. That is quite a loss and it came about because of their guarantee. That information may be found on page 34 of the public accounts.
What is going to happen because the lending companies have refused to lend this money? Somebody suggested that they were on strike. That was a very good term to use, but the minister objected to it; therefore I will not press the point. The fact is they are not lending the amount of money that they did before, and they are beginning to tighten up still further.
If that is the only source of money, and they refuse to lend it, how are you going to build these houses for the people in the low income brackets to whom the Minister of Resources and Development referred a while ago?
I suppose it would not be right to criticize the government, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the lending companies if I did not have something to suggest. It is common practice in this house to criticize the government and then not offer some solution to the problem. I have some suggestions. I would suggest first that you get rid of that white elephant, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It has been riding on the backs of the already overburdened taxpayers long enough. It may have had a purpose in days gone by, but I think that purpose has been served, and we could get on very well without it. One of the main purposes of Central Mortgage and Housing was to see that the building standards laid down under the National Housing Act were followed out. That has never been done in the majority of cases.
I can recall when these projects first started. Wherever you found difficulty it was in the lack of proper inspection. Mind you, Central Mortgage and Housing never did take the attitude, so far as I know, and certainly the officials to whom I have been speaking never interpreted their duties in that way, that they were to supply inspectors and see that the house was built according to the plans and specifications. What they were to do was to see that the house was built to their satisfaction. They thought that was all that was necessary. When I pointed out on many occasions that inferior cement, 68108-264
National Housing Act
material and workmanship were employed in a house, Central Mortgage and1 Housing authorities said: "Well, it is to our satisfaction."
The hon. member for Red Deer spoke of a project in Namao, Alberta, the other day. The difficulty arose there where Central Mortgage and Housing was supervising. The inspection was poor. I have said on many occasions-and I have said this to the minister -I do not think the federal government can supervise building construction all over Canada. It is just too big a job. Experience has proven that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is unable to do the job as far as proper building inspection is concerned.
I am told-I do not know how true it is1- they have even fired some of the good inspectors.
They were too honest.
I am not going to argue that point.
They did their work too well.

I did talk to an inspector who passed a house for the government. The plans called for No. 1 flooring. The floor was covered with paper, and it was a poor No. 2 flooring. He passed that house for the government. I said to him: "Did you not see the floor?" He said: "It was covered with paper."
They paid for No. 1.

Yes. That fellow was never fired. He should have been booted off the job. An old trick like that has whiskers on it. It is an old trick to have a floor covered with paper, have the government inspector come in, walk over the paper and pass the house. That was not an isolated case at all. There has never been proper inspection in the many cases that I can recall. I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that we get rid of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and in its place set up another type of organization. I recall that not long ago-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have been searching the records long enough now to have accumulated some evidence on what has really happened in the past in the discussion of the resolution amending the National Housing Act. Before one o'clock, while the hon. member for Eglinton was speaking, a lot of argument took place on the latitude which had been allowed in the past on a resolution of this kind. Therefore I did not see fit to stop any other hon. member until I could ascertain for myself what had been the practice. I have had all the Hansards since 1949 brought in

National Housing Act
to me and I have looked them all up to see what the procedure had been in the past on the resolutions preceding an amending bill of the National Housing Act. I find that a discussion wide in scope covering the whole of the national housing problem in Canada took place only when the minister himself chose to make general observations as to the problem before he commented specifically on the measure which was to follow the resolution. I find, too, that in committee I had to intervene and ask the hon. member for Eglinton to confine his remarks to the subject matter of the resolution. Of course at that time debate was permitted on the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair to go into committee of the whole on the resolution.
In the second year the bill was introduced in the Senate. It was not a money bill, and therefore when it came here it received first reading, and there was hardly any debate at all. The minister just made an explanatory statement. There was not much debate on second reading either, and a few observations on third reading. Therefore I think it would be quite proper for us now to agree to limit our observations to the resolution before the committee.
In this connection I would refer hon. members to page 1767 of Hansard for November 15, 1949, where the minister, moving second reading of Bill 142 of that session, said:
Before commenting upon the proposed legislation I should like to make some general remarks, including a few references to what has been achieved in the field of housing by the aggregate efforts of all who have concerned themselves with this important activity.
At that moment, although we had before us only an amending bill, because the minister chose to make a general statement on the problems of housing in Canada, we had a general debate. But, later on in committee, that debate was restricted to the terms of the resolution itself. My words on that occasion were to the following effect, that, as the resolution before the committee dealt with amendments to the National Housing Act, I must ask the hon. member who was then speaking to confine himself to that resolution.
In other words, these records show that in the committee on the resolution, so far as possible the debate was confined to the subject matter of the resolution. But when Mr. Speaker was in the chair, on the motion that he leave the chair, the debate had been general in scope because the minister had made a general statement.

I understood the objection taken when the hon. member for Eglinton was speaking was that he was referring to a specific case. I have not been referring to specific cases at all. The resolution under
IThe Chairman.]
discussion is that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944. That is the language about which I am arguing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member will have to add that it is to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, in certain particulars. I stopped the hon. member for Eglinton this morning when he was referring to the cost of the building which now shelters the National Housing Act administration and, secondly, when he referred to a certain project now undertaken by a lending institution and, I think, guaranteed by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I stopped him in those two instances. Since that time I have been checking the record to ascertain whether or not in committee on these resolutions debate of the whole national housing problem has taken place. I find to my satisfaction that that has not been the case.
One opportunity for debate is now eliminated because of Mr. Speaker's ruling of recent date which states that on the motion for Mr. Speaker to leave the chair there shall be no debate. Therefore in committee we must follow the procedure which has been followed in the past, at least since 1949, and that is that discussion must be strictly relevant to the resolution, and the proposed amendments contemplated by the resolution and the bill to follow.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps there may be cases when the ruling you have just made would be applicable, and would prove the point you have now attempted to make. It seems to me, however, that this resolution is in an entirely different position from most of those to which you have been referring, because as I see it this one does allow for a general discussion, and for the simple reason that in this resolution we are dealing with an increase in the appropriation in respect of loans provided by section 7 of the act, such increase to be from $300 million to $500 million. Then, in addition to that, there is provision whereby under part II there shall be an increase from $150 million to $250 million.
I suggest that when the minister introduces these increases in the appropriation, at the same time he opens the way for debate on matters which would be covered by that increase. It seems to me this opens the subject matter pretty wide, and I suggest that the chairman ought to be very careful in not trying to restrict discussion, in view of the fact that these appropriations are being made for those very things hon. members have been discussing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not wish to prolong discussion on a matter of procedure. I fully realize that if we do not have the co-operation of hon. members-in other words, if hon. members have made up their minds that they are going to make general speeches in respect to housing on this resolution-I do not see how I can stop them. I am free to confess that; because in debating a similar resolution in the past I have known occasions where, for instance, certain hon. members have argued that unless they were given a statement of policy in the matter of rent control they were not prepared to proceed with a debate amending the National Housing Act.
Any number of arguments can be made. If hon. members wish to discuss national housing problems generally on this resolution, then I do not think I can stop them, because we will just keep on arguing every time an hon. member rises. We will hear the argument that what he has to say is relevant, and that it has to do with what takes place under the National Housing Act. But I would ask hon. members to remember this, that so far as the performance of my duties here is concerned, I am tied by two directives, the first of which is found in that standing order which says that discussions in committee of the whole shall be strictly relevant to the resolution under debate. The second is the citation from Beauchesne's third edition, to which I referred this morning, and which says that the resolution in committee is merely indicative of what the bill is going to be, and that at this stage we are merely deciding as to the advisability of making certain expenditures.
Confined within those limits, all I can do is to ask the co-operation of hon. members. If they feel they should discuss cases concerning contractors who have not built properly, or if they feel they should discuss the building of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation on the Montreal road, or if they wish to cover the whole field covered by the National Housing Act, all I can say is that I will hold in my mind the view that they are going far afield from the amendments suggested in this resolution.
Having said that, I shall ask hon. members to carry on the debate, having in mind that they should restrict rather than increase the latitude of discussion.

I shall try to keep within your ruling; I always do. Indeed, I thought I was doing exceptionally well, and that I was staying within your ruling by not referring to any special cases. I had plenty of them in mind, 1 may say.
One of the things the Prime Minister indicated some time ago was that he did not think the federal government should become
National Housing Act
landlords for the people of Canada. I agree with him wholeheartedly. But I think we are rapidly approaching the position where we are going to be landlords, unless some changes are made.
I suggest there is a way out of that difficulty. My first suggestion would be to get rid of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If they have performed a duty in the past, then that duty has been fulfilled, and we should pension them off, or take whatever procedure would seem to be best fitted to the process of getting rid of them.
The second thing I think should be done is that the government should set up a revolving fund of, let us say, $500 million-and 1 am not saying what the exact amount should be-and that these sums of money should be lent to the municipalities at a rate of interest not exceeding 2 per cent. I mentioned a moment ago that Alberta had had outstanding good luck in the repayment of money to the revolving fund they had set up. Something like $460,000 had been paid back, and up to date they have not lost a cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Does the hon. member know what the Alberta government has done by way of restricting their legislation this year in that field?

As I indicated a moment ago, the only information I have is from a report of the budget speech by the premier of Alberta. It seems to me that he has gone even farther than that. I should like to quote from the Ottawa Citizen of March 7, 1953, where they give an account of Mr. Manning's budget speech, which reads in part:
He also had good news for those municipalities finding it hard to keep their services in step with their growing population. He gave details of a plan for a $25 million revolving fund, part of a broader scheme to share Alberta's increasing revenues with the municipalities.
That is in addition to the $17 million I was speaking of a while ago in connection with which they had already received back $460,000 from the self liquidating projects. If a province like Alberta can put aside $25 million from their budget to provide a revolving fund to assist the municipalities in these self-liquidating projects, the federal government could set up a revolving fund of, say, $500 million to be loaned to the municipalities, through the provinces of course. I recognize immediately that there has to be some control over this money and the proper control would be through the province to the municipality.
It seems to me that that would immediately relieve the federal government of the burden of having to supervise the construction of these houses. That would then become the responsibility of the municipality. That would
4168

National Housing Act
mean that municipalities-I am thinking particularly of Calgary-would not permit the type of construction that has been allowed under the National Housing Act. I think the best thing that could happen would be to have the responsibility of seeing that these houses are properly constructed according to the plans and specifications, laid down by the federal government if you like in conjunction with the provincial governments, placed on the municipalities. The onus would be taken off the back of the Minister of Resources and Development, and I imagine that he would like to get rid of that responsibility.
On the other hand, the municipalities could set up construction committees. There is not a municipality in Canada where competent contractors and builders could not be found. Competent construction committees could be set up and would be right on the job to see that the plans and specifications were carried out in the interests of the person who was going to buy the house. You would then not have the outrageous examples we have had of poor inspection. Certainly under a system like that the government could not possibly lose more than they lost last year, when according to the public accounts they lost $686,000. Alberta lost nothing with their revolving fund. I do not think we would lose any money at all, and the responsibility would be on the municipality, where it should be, to see that the construction was carried out according to the plans and specifications.
That brings up the problem mentioned by the minister when he was speaking to the Appraisal Institute of Canada. How are you going to make it possible for people with small incomes to get houses? As I said a moment ago, the home is the best security you could have for money. The down payment could be made as low as $500 and there would still be sufficient equity in the house to cover what was owing on it at any time. Then a small monthly payment could be set to take care of the upkeep and deterioration of the property, unless the government was intending to go into a money-making scheme, and I do not think that is its intention.
I have just been handed a clipping from the Edmonton Journal of March 3, 1953, which states that last year the city of Edmonton received a loan of $1 million from the fund. In the three years the fund has been in existence Edmonton has borrowed $3,900,000. That answers the question the minister asked a minute ago. It would appear that the fund is being continued.
Let me get back to the other point. I think the monthly payment could be made quite

small, possibly no more than $25, $30 or $35 for low-priced houses. That is only an estimate. The amount would have to be figured out over a period of years. That would meet the difficulty we have been running up against over the past few years. It would certainly meet the difficulties mentioned by some of the speakers this afternoon. It would give definite relief to the municipalities; it would increase home building by the lower income groups, which is what we all greatly desire; it would result in the building of better homes; there would be a smaller loss by the federal government; we would get away from the tremendous cost of keeping up Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation; the federal government would get rid of a terrific headache and the people would get better homes. It seems to me that it would be a better plan all the way through.
I do not suppose the federal government will pay any attention to this. I may be entirely wrong in what I have said, but at least the government cannot say that we have not offered some alternative. This is not something that has been tried and has failed. Quite the contrary, this revolving fund idea has been found to be of the greatest success. As I suggested, the home is the last thing that a man will let out of his grasp if he can possibly hang on. It is one of the first things that we should see the Canadian people have. I believe that with a proper organization to carry this out we would have much greater success in our national housing program.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: I would like to deal with one or two of the points raised by the hon. member for Bow River. I think there are misunderstandings which led to several statements he made. The amount of the loan under the joint loan technique is no longer related to the lending value; rather it is related to the agreed sales price. That was one of the points upon which the hon. member based an argument.
Is that the present sales price? If so there still is no difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
The agreed sales price at the present time, yes. Builders in Alberta and elsewhere are building and selling houses at prices lower than the agreed sales price, the agreed sales price being the figure agreed upon in the first instance by the builder and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, jointly with the lending institution, before there is qualification for the 80 per cent loan.
There are some areas in Canada where difficulty is being experienced with the agreed sales price, but with most builders and in most areas in Canada the technique is working satisfactorily and it has proved to be a good weapon in the fight against inflation.

The hon. member dealt today, as he has on many occasions-I am always glad to receive his criticism-with the inspection of houses, and he related his remarks to the standards under the National Housing Act and said they were too low.

I did not say they were too low; the point was that they were not being lived up to, no matter what they were. I think the standards set by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the National Housing Act are fairly good provided they are lived up to.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: I am glad the hon. member has cleared up that point, because most of the criticism we hear is that we are requiring people to build to too high a standard rather than too low a standard. Regarding inspections under the joint loan technique it is for the lending institution to satisfy itself that the mortgage value is there in respect of the money it is lending.

Where does Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation come in? I quite understand that it is for the lending institution to satisfy itself that the value is there, but where does the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation inspection come in?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Under the joint loan technique, inspections are made by the lending institution. Central Mortgage, of course, are concerned to the extent that they put up 25 per cent of the mortgage money. They inspect in order to see that their participation in that mortgage money is protected, but it is not their responsibility to make an architectural or construction inspection. Under that arrangement, such is the responsibility of the owner of the house.

I do not like to keep interrupting the minister all the time, but I should like to get this point cleared up. Whose responsibility is it, then, to see that the houses are build according to the plans and specifications set out under the N.H.A.?

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: It is the responsibility of the home owner to ensure that he is getting what he has bought from the builder. We have discussed this point on many occasions in this house.
The owner has no say.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member then dealt with aid to municipalities. I do agree with him that this is a very important matter if we are to have a large program of house building in this country. It was for that reason that we put section 35 on the statute books. We did that only after talking to all provincial governments. The
National Housing Act
hon. member holds up Alberta as the criterion and says we should take a lesson from that province. Well, Mr. Chairman, the last thing I would want to do is be critical of any provincial government. I would say, however, that if we took a lesson from Alberta in the field of housing, I think there would be many people in Canada who would not be too happy about the housing policy.

I did not suggest you take a lesson from my province in the matter of building houses, because that has not been their function. It has been the function of the federal government to do that. What I did point out was the experience Alberta had in regard to this revolving fund for self-liquidating projects.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
Obviously the hon. member is under a considerable number of misapprehensions, and this is another one of them. I do not think we should get into a debate on the matter at this particular time. I would be glad to deal more specifically with this point on my estimates, which should be under consideration very soon.
It is not the responsibility of the federal government to build houses. Under the British North America Act housing is the responsibility of provincial governments, because it is a matter of property and civil rights. The basic policy of the federal government is to enable people to build houses by making available the proper economic climate, and by doing what it can within its own sphere of influence to make credit available.
Now, the Alberta government has a revolving fund. One of the techniques the federal government has at its disposal is co-operation with the provincial governments, and we do that under section 35. As I understand it the Alberta legislation was amended this year to discontinue having money from that revolving fund flow into municipal works through section 35. If a municipality wishes to benefit by the co-operative plan under section 35 it must now go into the open market to get its money. The Alberta revolving fund is no longer available. I do not wish to be critical of the government on that point. They probably did that because they felt it was in the best interests of the people they served. I merely cite that as a matter of fact.
The hon. member is critical of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I am not denying him that right to be critical. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation was set up to serve the interests of the people of Canada, and to the extent it is doing that I think the people of Canada will approve. So far, it is a fact that Central Mortgage and

National Housing Act
Housing Corporation has put some $343 million into the financial stream to assist housing in this country. I am satisfied in my own mind that this amount would not have gone into housing had there not been a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I think all hon. members know that under the joint loan technique, which is the major operation under the National Housing Act, the basic loan is 80 per cent of the agreed sales price and the amortization period can run to 30 years. The lending institutions, if they were operating alone, would make a loan of 60 per cent as the maximum; that is, there would be a down payment of 40 per cent required. The amortization period would be of the order of ten years. The interest rate instead of being 5J per cent as it is now, because federal money goes into that partnership arrangement on a 3J per cent interest rate, I am satisfied would be at least 6 per cent. The lending institutions put their money in now at 5i per cent on an 80 per cent basis because the pool guarantee is there for their protection. If there were no pool guarantee and each loan were made on what is called the conventional basis, I am satisfied the interest rate would be a minimum of 6 per cent as I have said.
Through the government's operations under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and in addition to this vast amount of money that has flowed into housing, there has been a substantial saving to each householder in Canada or each tenant in Canada who is living in accommodation which was built under some arrangement in which Central Mortgage and Housing participated. I consider that the corporation has done a good job. It is natural 1 should feel that way because I am responsible to parliament for the operation of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The more I see of their operations, the more I am satisfied that they are doing a good service for the people of Canada and that the taxpayers are getting their money's worth from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I feel that the corporation is being administered in a manner that is eminently satisfactory to the vast majority of the taxpayers in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that even by the widest stretch of imagination could this government really believe that it is dealing adequately with the present housing situation either by this amendment or by any measure which it has introduced during the past two years. I intend very briefly to show where I think the government has fallen down, and to show what additional steps I believe the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should take in order to
IMr. Winters.]
make it possible for the construction industry to build the houses which it is capable of building, and to enable those who desperately need housing, to purchase it.
First of all, what is the situation today? We have in Canada today a shortage of half a million unbuilt and much-needed houses. This housing shortage is growing greater every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Would the hon. member say on what he bases that estimate?
Yes; I was hoping the minister would ask that. On page 12, clause 17 of the report of the advisory committee on reconstruction, commonly known as the Curtis report-
What year?
I was getting to the year.
I was afraid you were not.

I would not miss such an important thing. On page 12, clause 17 of the report of the advisory committee on reconstruction, known as the Curtis report, concerning housing and planning, dated March 24, 1944, we find that the total urban housing backlog in 1944 was estimated to be 320,000 houses. I might add that this was a government-sponsored survey.
According to the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, since that year we have built 663,500 new houses. Also, from the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics, we have added 710,400 new families to our population. That means that our backlog of housing has increased by 46,900 during the past eight years.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Might I ask if those figures of family formations are arrived at by taking the figures for each year and totalling them?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Do they have regard to wastage over the years?
Yes, I have here figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics for each of the eight years from 1944 to the end of 1952, and they list these figures as net new family formations.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: For each year?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: Then you total them by years?
This is the total for the eight years. If the minister would like, I will give him the total for each year.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
I am just interested in knowing how you get the figure, whether you took the figures for each year and totalled them,

or whether the bulk figure has regard to wastage through emigration and so on.
Well, the word "net" in the expression "net family formations" takes that into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: For each year?
For each single year. We total the figures for the eight years and that gives us a figure of 710,400 new families which have been added to our population in the last eight years.
What about families which have left?

I was going on to say that our backlog of housing has increased by 46,900 during the past eight years. That figure, however, does not take into account the number of new houses needed to replace those which have become useless due to obsolescence. On page 12, clause 19 of the Curtis report, that figure is estimated to be 13,500 per year, and again this is an estimate given by a government-sponsored survey.
Therefore between 1944 and 1952 the total number of houses which should have been replaced amounted to 121,500. Adding that figure to the 320,000 backlog accumulated prior to 1944, and to the 46,900 surplus of new families over house construction between 1944 and 1952, we arrive at a total backlog of 488,400, or roughly half a million houses.
I would like to give as an example the situation in the year just passed, 1952. According to the bureau of statistics, during that year we produced 73,087 houses. Net new families formed during last year were 93,000. Therefore we have a surplus of new families formed over houses produced of 20,000. If we take the estimate of the Curtis report that the number of houses that should have been replaced due to obsolescence during the last year was 13,500, we find that during last year alone we should have produced 33,500 more houses than we did produce, if we were merely to keep pace with new family formations and replacement through obsolescence.
The next thing I would like to examine is the possibility for additional construction, and I would like to quote the opinions of several people who I think are best qualified to express opinions on this matter. First of all I would like to quote from what Mr. P. G. Wilmut, president of the Canadian Construction Association, said in his presidential address to the association in Montreal on January 19, 1953. He said that the Canadian construction industry should consider 125,000 houses a year as a normal minimum target to be aimed at. That opinion is concurred in by the Canadian house builders' association,
National Housing Act
and also by Dr. Firestone, economic adviser to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He said in Toronto on February 19, 1951, that the productive capacity of the Canadian construction industry could conceivably rise to
130,000	houses per year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, from all this, two things I believe are apparent. First of all, we have a backlog of unbuilt and much needed houses numbering half a million. We also have a potential production capacity of from 125,000 to 130,000 houses per year. That opinion has been expressed by those best able to calculate the productive capacity of the Canadian construction industry. However, we find that during the past year we built only 73,000 houses, when we could have built 70 per cent more.
We naturally have to ask ourselves: Why did this take place? I believe it was caused by three things. First is the lack of serviced land. The second factor is that the down payment required by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is too high; and, third, the interest rate charged on Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages is too high and the amortization period over which loans must be paid off is too short.
I would first like to deal with the question of serviced land. A great many municipalities today simply cannot afford to provide the schools and the local improvements which are necessary to go with a housing development. I think it is common sense that you simply cannot build houses unless the municipality permits you to build the houses within the municipality. In connection with this difficulty I believe the Leader of the Opposition made a very excellent suggestion on November 24 last as recorded on page 33 of Hansard. He urged the government, and I quote his words:
To reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined re-allocation of taxing powers, so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
I believe if that suggestion were followed out we would overcome the difficulties with which municipalities are faced in finding resources with which they could finance the building of schools and local improvements.
The second difficulty with which I want to deal is the 20 per cent down payment which is required on all N.H.A. houses. The cheapest house one can buy through N.H.A. costs $10,000, so the down payment which one must put up is $2,000. In order to find that $2,000 I believe one must earn a minimum salary of $5,000 a year for a minimum of four years. Even then it requires the setting aside

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext: I think the hon. member knows that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation does not charge 5} per cent.
No; I mean the mortgages obtained through Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Resources and Development
speechtext:
Through the lending
institution.

Through the lending institution. This rate of interest, and the time over which it is necessary to pay off the loan, make it impossible for a person with a low income to carry the charges on a new house.
Again I should like to examine what has been done in the United States. In that country, under their national housing authority, mortgages are made available at rates as low as 4 per cent, and they can be paid off over a period of as long as 30 years. I believe this policy merits serious consideration by the government because, in the United States, it permits people with moderate incomes to carry the charges on a new house. In Canada a policy similar to that would make it possible for a man earning between $55 and $60 a week to carry the charges on a good new house.
If the government persists in following what I honestly believe is an obsolete and reactionary housing policy, I believe the situation is going to continue to grow worse every day. As I pointed out, last year the situation deteriorated by a further 33,500

house shortage. As I have also pointed out, the accumulated shortage today amounts to half a million houses. If this situation is allowed to continue to deteriorate, families with four and five children are going to be forced to continue to live in one room. I shall be pleased to take the minister, any time he comes to Toronto, to see accommodation in which families with four and five children are living in one room and paying up to $60 a month rent just because they have no other place in which to live. I do not believe these conditions are the kind in which we can permit Canadians to live.
As I say, it would be one thing if the situation were just a temporary one, but it is not that at all. The situation is getting worse every single day, and the government is showing no inclination to right the situation and to permit the building industry to build the houses which it is capable of building.
I believe the government must immediately reconsider its housing policy in view of three things: First, the chronic housing shortage which is increasing every day; second, the proved ability of the Canadian construction industry to build almost double the number of houses it is building today, if given the opportunity to do so; and third, the success which has been achieved in the United States through practical housing policies which have made housing available to families which need it most.

I should like to say a few words on this matter, Mr. Chairman, whether I say them now or on second reading of the bill. They are of a general nature, and as the debate has been fairly general I think possibly we would be saving time if I continued at this stage.
Last year when speaking on the question of housing I made four recommendations to the government which were as follows: first, that all municipal taxation be allowed as a deduction from income for taxation purposes; second, that personal expenditures on the education of one's own family be allowed as a deduction irrespective of age; third, that mortgage interest payments on the dwelling lived in by the taxpayer be allowed as a similar deduction; and fourth, the calling of a conference of all provincial ministers of education and housing with the federal government to discuss the whole question of housing.
Since that time I have tried to find out what these suggestions would mean and whether there was any support whatever for them. I took the trouble to go into my own riding and make a survey; it was a

small survey, nevertheless it was a survey. It covered some 70 householders who were in the new section of the riding. I wanted to find out what these would mean to the individuals in a new housing development.
I came up with these average figures. I might explain to the committee that this is merely a small sampling, but it is a sampling of a new development, one which has been built since the war and which contains a large percentage of veterans and a large percentage of young families.
The figures I have are as follows. The average cost of the house was $13,000. If both mortgage payments and municipal taxation had been allowed as a deduction from income, the average deduction would be of the nature of $190. I am not giving the figures to the closest dollar or the closest cent but to the nearest $10. In this group the average income tax paid was $525. If the mortgage payment were not allowed and if only the municipal taxation were allowed, the saving of the average home owner in this group would be $47.50 a year.
I mention these figures, Mr. Chairman, because I think they are indicative of what can be expected if a proposal such as this is carried out. It would mean a saving of 19 per cent in the average income tax. I asked whether there was any support for my proposal either from the building side of housing or from the lending side, and I must say that I have received quite a bit of support-not all of it directly, though some of it was actually directly-from the lending side of the picture, that is to say, from organizations whose duty it is to lend money particularly for housing purposes. In this connection I should like to quote one paragraph from the annual statement of the Chartered Trust Company, which contains the text of an address by Rolph R. Corson, who is the president of the corporation which is certainly concerned with the lending of money, particularly on mortgages. He said this at the annual meeting of the company, and I think it is interesting enough to quote the two short paragraphs to the committee. It is headed: "Inequity in income tax." It reads as follows:
All the trust companies are in the mortgage business and before I close there is one inequity in present income tax rulings that, if continued, may have an unfavourable bearing on our national economy. The trust companies have reason to remember the effect of mortgage moratoriums in the 1930's and the necessity for the removal of the contributing causes. To deal with the shortage of houses the National Housing Act was enacted. It allows people of limited means to purchase needed homes with a small down payment and give back a much larger mortgage than is considered safe by the government for a trustee
National Housing Act
investment. Today's price for houses is two or three times greater than a few years ago, and the mortgage load much heavier. For thousands of young people starting their family life, a roof overhead, no matter what its cost, is a "must". Ownership of property carries a municipal tax obligation, which is also heavier than formerly, and today's higher interest rate on a larger mortgage adds to an already heavy load.
Under present conditions this act was a move in the right direction, but it did not go far enough to accomplish its end. Municipal taxes and interest payments at least should have been allowed as an income tax deduction. Certainly the heavier load assumed by the home owner under this act should be carefully considered and lightened as much as possible. In the United States, where they also have a housing problem, they have met it more realistically as both municipal taxes and mortgage interest are allowed.
So much for the lending institutions. I come now to two resolutions passed by the Canadian association of real estate boards at their convention last fall in Toronto. The minister has probably seen this, but I will just quote the resolutions and the four-line preamble to the first one which is this:
Whereas this increase in municipal property taxation is due to the rapidly accelerating cost of education, social welfare and other items, which are not services rendered to property, and should rightfully be borne by the population as a whole, therefore
Be it resolved that the government of Canada be urged in the strongest possible terms to permit, in the national interest, the deduction of municipal property taxes from the taxable personal income of owners of single family dwellings, as a means of making home ownership economically possible for even the lowest income group.
These are two authorities which I submit have considerable experience and knowledge of the problem of housing and the provision of houses for rapidly growing communities.
With respect to this question of mortgage money, a pernicious system has grown up in districts where conditions are not completely in conformity with the national housing regulations. I may say that these regulations are pretty rigid. There are many cases where young families are building their own houses, doing a great deal of the work on them themselves, but which do not rigidly and completely conform to the regulations. It may be that they are outside the area where the lending organizations will lend money, or for some other technical reason; nevertheless they find themselves outside the regulations, and they are forced to go not to the larger lending institutions but to other sources of capital.
It has been found that a system of what you might call bonus or premium mortgages has cropped up. The system works roughly this way. A home owner wishing $6,000 goes to a source of capital and that source of capital says: "Very well, I will lend you the money at 5J or 6 per cent interest. But instead of

National Housing Act
signing a mortgage for $6,000 you will sign a mortgage for $7,500, and there will be $1,500 capital bonus to me for accommodating you with these funds." In other words there is water in the mortgage to the extent of 15 per cent, 20 per cent and sometimes even more. Quite a lot of people have come to me with that problem. I think it is pernicious, and everything should be done to stop it.
The question of serviced land is also an important one. It arises in rapidly-growing municipalities around Toronto and in many other metropolitan areas as well. A municipality finds itself virtually unable to provide serviced land, to instal the physical services Such as water mains, storm sewers, sanitary sewers, street lights, pavements, sidewalks, police and fire services and all the other amenities. They cost at the very minimum about $5,000 an acre. Assume that you can build between four and five houses on an acre. It means that you have a capital cost, before you turn a sod to build your house, of around $1,000 and possibly more.
On top of that cost there is the capital cost 6f schools. Today, depending of course on the new family formation density and many other things, I would certainly hazard as a reasonable guess that the cost of schools and the cost of servicing land therefor would add another $1,000 per acre. That is merely the provision of the physical plant. It does not take into account any question of amortization. The amortization of the school board debentures and the cost of the upkeep of the school merely adds to the interest charges of operation. Therefore, before the first sod is turned for a new house, if there is a density of four and a half or five to the acre-and that is reasonable-there is a capital cost of approximately $2,000 per house.
Some way must be found of meeting that capital cost. At the present time, with the lending powers of municipalities considerably stretched, particularly those municipalities with a high percentage of housing and a low percentage of industry, as is found in many metropolitan areas, the borrowing power or the credit of municipalities is taxed to the point where they have to pay 5, 5J and sometimes 5J or even 6 per cent for their money.
This, of course, is a direct charge on the home owner, and a direct charge on the head of the family. What can be done about it? In the United States the banking system is entirely different from ours. They have commercial banks; and then, in a separate category, they have savings banks. These savings banks are rapidly growing institutions, operating under the safeguards of the bank insur-
ance protection enacted by the federal authorities after the bank holiday in 1933. I would judge them to be wholly solvent and sound institutions.
Through the provisions under which they operate, these savings banks are in the mortgage business and are permitted to lend money. Our chartered banks in Canada are not permitted to do that; and I would not for one moment suggest that they should go into the mortgage business. But how are we going to get that money into the hands of the municipalities so that schools and serviced lands can be provided?
I am going to make a suggestion, and I make it on my own behalf. In doing so I am not speaking for anyone other than myself. My suggestion is that some consideration should be given to allowing municipalities, under strict regulation, to issue tax-free bonds. I know this suggestion flies against a great deal of conservative thought-and I use the word with a small "c". No doubt there are many objections to this procedure, but we must keep in mind that we are not dealing with a situation as it prevailed before the war. Rather we are dealing with an entirely new situation, a condition under which large amounts of surplus funds, either of corporations or of individuals, are siphoned off by corporation and individual income taxes. So the formation of capital today is not, on a percentage basis, anywhere near as great as it was before the war. So much for that subject.
The municipality today is the creature of the province. I should think that it must continue to be the creature of the province, as well as its responsibility. But because of the high incidence of taxation, because of the high-geared income and corporation tax we are finding that the municipality is being driven into a more and more difficult position. This very condition introduced in the budget this year, under which we have a 20 per cent tax credit from the income from common and preferred stocks-which are called equities-is going to mean that the average private investor will find himself less and less likely to invest in corporation bonds. And in order to equal the attractiveness or the yield of the common stock, to an investor who is in the income tax bracket anywhere above 15 per cent-and today that is a comparatively low bracket-any investor is going to have to get at least 1J per cent or probably 2 per cent more on a bond than he would get on a common stock, in order to make the yield equal irrespective of the growth possibilities of the common and sometimes even the preferred stock.

The effect of that will be felt, and I feel that the effect on the borrowing power of the municipality is going to be very serious.
I would think that, in order to sell them, the yield on municipal securities must be increased. Having said that and, as I have intimated, having spoken for myself alone,
I feel a conference should be called between ministers of education and ministers of finance of the different provinces, to see if something cannot be worked out. The old shibboleths as to what cannot be done should be forgotten or at least, for the moment, put to one side.
We have here a problem that is not being solved by our present methods. The machinery is inadequate. Insecurity, particularly if there is any slight recession in earnings or even moderate unemployment, will grow at a very rapid rate. As has been said, aside from national defence there is nothing as important today as providing for the security of tenure, the security of a man's hearth and home. Next to his life, and the security of his country, these are the most important things he has.
I believe we should look at these matters in a new light so as to try to find ways and means whereby the load will be taken off municipalities through the liberalization of terms of borrowing. But not by increasing the scope of the municipal taxing power. As the load is taken off municipalities it is immediately taken off the home owner who has to pay for the servicing of the debt.
