AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 186, to amend the Canada Grain Act (distribution of box cars).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide a fair method by which 
box cars may be allocated among elevator companies at marketing points in western Canada. The purpose of this bill is to meet a situation which has grown up in which there is no effective competition in the buying of grain from prairie producers. The bill itself is very simple. The first clause reads as follows:
Any producer, as defined In section 12 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, may, before the first day of October in any year, enter in the car order book his acreage seeded to grain as shown in his permit book pursuant to sections 15 and 16 of the said act, and may assign that acreage among the elevator companies at his marketing point.
This would allow the farmer to take his permit book to the railway agent and, in a new section of the car order book provided for this purpose, state his seeded acreage and declare the elevator company through which he wishes to market his grain.
The second paragraph of the bill provides that the amendment would be operative only if the car order book was not being used. The car order book is part of the Canada Grain Act. The Canada Grain Act includes a provision for the car order book, which provision was obtained by western producers after many years of struggle with various federal governments. The producers feel that the Canada Grain Act is their charter.
I for one would not feel capable of altering the act from its original purposes. However,
I do believe that the provision I have suggested would provide a satisfactory method by which farmers by their own choice may provide a means of allocating box cars amongst the elevator companies. I believe this amendment would improve the act considerably.
As I say, under the present situation there is no effective competition in the buying of grain. Before we had this large surplus in western Canada, and when elevator companies had excess space available in each crop year, a farmer could go into one elevator and if he believed his grain were No. 2 but the agent would pay him only for No. 3 he could go out of that elevator and to the next elevator company to see if that agent might give him a better grade. Under the situation now prevailing often all the elevator companies at any given point are plugged. Possibly one elevator might get a couple of box cars, and the agent will announce that he is prepared to buy 4,000 bushels of wheat the following day. The farmers, whether or not they prefer to take their grain to another elevator company, are almost certain to haul their grain to that elevator because they are in need of funds to carry on their farming operations and pay their living costs.

As I say, for a number of years the situation has been entirely different from normal. One might argue that we should not amend the Canada Grain Act because the present surplus of wheat in this country is going to be taken care of in a year or so. Then we would not need this type of amendment. I say that if any member of this house makes a study of the wheat supplies on hand in the various exporting countries of the world today he cannot help but come to the conclusion that we are faced with a world glut of wheat. When I looked over the statistics I was amazed at the huge quantities of wheat on hand in the various exporting countries.
According to the latest publication of the dominion bureau of statistics, "The Wheat Review" for March, on March 1 of this year the four major exporting countries of the world had on -hand for export and carryover-that is the quantity of wheat in addition to that needed for domestic consumption, feed for livestock and seed supplies-the huge total of 1,468 million bushels. From that date until the end of the crop year, under the present international wheat agreement there is an unfilled quota of some 135 million bushels. In other words, after taking into account the quantity of wheat that is to be delivered under the present international wheat agreement, and taking into account the probable total that may be sold as class II wheat, the four major exporting countries of the world will have something like 1,200 million bushels of wheat on hand for export on July 31 of this year.
It was for this reason that I, for one, hoped that the international wheat agreement would be signed by all the countries and would become effective. Even if the wheat agreement is signed by all countries there will be on hand on July 31 of this year sufficient wheat for the exporting countries to cover more than two full years of the allocations under that agreement. If these exporting countries produce little or no wheat in the next two years for export purposes, there is still sufficient wheat available in those countries to cover two full years of operation under the international wheat agreement. I suggest, therefore, that the present surplus wheat condition in Canada, the plugged elevators, the wheat available on farms which the farmers are unable to market, is a condition that is likely to continue for a number of years ahead. If Canada and the other exporting countries get even a normal crop this year, with the surplus situation as it is, I think it is essential that something be done to improve the allocation and distribution of box cars.
As a matter of fact if Canada this year sells as much wheat as she sold in the export
Canada Grain Act
markets in the record year, Canada will wind up with a carryover of some 330 million bushels, which will be the largest peacetime carryover in the history of the country. -Canada and the world are, therefore, faced with a large glut of wheat. This situation of filled elevators, a shortage of transportation facilities and farmers ready to market grain without the facilities being available, is likely to continue for some time to come. In such a situation I feel that something more should be done to provide a better distribution of -box cars than anything that has been tried to date.
We have a transport controller. As I understand his position and the work he does, he does not allocate box cars among the elevator companies at individual marketing points. What happens is that the local elevator agents daily send to the wheat board a record of the purchases they have made and the shipments from the elevator, if any, as well as the amount of storage space available. The wheat board then sends this information to the transport controller, together with the quotas that prevail at the various marketing points. On the basis of this information the transport controller then says to the railway companies that there is a certain area in western Canada that needs box cars. Box -cars are then sent, shall we say, to 100 marketing points; but after that the distribution of box cars as between the elevator companies is entirely the responsibility of the railway companies themselves.
As so often happens you may have one elevator company, possibly a pool elevator company, to which 50 per cent of the farmers at that point wish to deliver their grain. You may have three other elevator companies that normally would allocate amongst themselves 50 per cent of the business; but when the railway companies send four box cars to that marketing point they do not give the popular elevator half of the box cars because half of the farmers want to deliver grain to the pool elevator. They say: Well, let us do it on a rough- rule of thumb basis; we will give each elevator company one box car. That immediately forces half of the pool customers to the other elevator companies. It is perfectly true that at certain points farmers will prefer to take their grain to the line elevator companies, and the same thing operates in reverse.
The bill I am proposing would allow the farmers early in the crop year, before October 1, to post their acreage in the car order book with the railway agent. Following that the railway agent at that marketing point would have to apportion the box cars among the elevator companies in the same way that farmers apportion their acreages among the elevator companies, as indicated by the entries

Canada Grain Act
in the car order book. If half the farmers with half of the seeded acreage desire to take their own grain to a certain elevator company then that elevator company, by this provision, must receive half of all box cars spotted at that marketing point.
I think anyone who believes in competition, who believes in freedom of choice, should support this bill; because in the marketing of grain now we have regimentation of the worst kind. The farmer must of financial necessity market his grain at whatever elevator may have been fortunate enough to get some box cars the night before and has a little elevator space available. This bill would allow the farmers themselves to indicate where they wish to market their grain, and as a result of that indication box cars would be allotted on that basis.
Somebody might say well, you can use the car order book system. However, I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will agree with me when I say that the car order book was not brought into effect to allocate and distribute box cars among elevator companies. The purpose of the car order book provision initially was to allow the farmer to order a car, in order to deliver over the platform a carload of a certain kind of grain that he might have, and get away from the necessity of selling it through local elevator facilities.
The car order book now is being used for a purpose for which it was not intended. I do not in any way blame the farmers for using the car order book as it is now being used. Certainly it is better than leaving the distribution of box cars to the railway agents or the railway companies at a great many points.
Wherever the pool elevator company, for example, feels that it has not been getting its fair share of box cars it will ask its farmers to go to the railway station and order cars through the car order book. Immediately, then, the car order book system comes into effect. It is easy for a large farmer who has a quota of 2,000 bushels of grain to deliver to order a box car, but for the smaller farmer who has a quota of 300, 400 or 500 bushels of grain to deliver the car order book is a very cumbersome procedure indeed. Many small farmers feel that the car order book has not been established for their use and they do not attempt to use it. In other instances they try to band together with a number of other small farmers and order a car amongst four, five or six farmers.
As I say, the car order book system when used as a method of distribution of box cars amongst elevator companies is very cumber-

some. In addition it led to a lot of friction at many elevator points when first put into effect. Sometimes you find a rush of large farmers, who want to sell their grain to a certain company, going into the same station on the same day at the same time and ordering perhaps 20 cars on the car order book. Then that elevator company will get the first 20 box cars and the other elevator companies will get none. The ordinary patrons of the other elevator companies will be pretty sore at their neighbours who filled the car order book for cars for that particular company.
The car order book provision is good and it has worked well when used for its original purpose; but it was never intended to be used as a method of allocating box cars among railway companies. Railway companies and farmers who use the car order book system as a method of allocating cars do so only in desperation when they have felt that grave injustice was being done in the distribution of cars by the railway companies at an elevator point.
There is another reason why I feel this bill should be accepted by the house. If I read the judgment aright, some of the protection that prevailed under the Canada Grain Act for a great many years has been removed by the recent decision of the board of transport commissioners in the Kreutzweiser case. As I read section 112 of the act, and as I know it has been used in years gone by, a farmer had the right to drive into an elevator company with his wheat and, if there was any dispute about the grade of his grain, he had the right to ask that the elevator company purchase that load of grain subject to grade in dockage. Samples of the grain were put in a tin receptacle provided for the purpose and sent to the chief inspector of grain at Winnipeg, and the sample came back with an official grade, and the farmer was entitled to the price for that official grade.
The judgment of the board of transport commissioners reads in part as follows:
The provisions of section 112 requiring a sample to be taken and placed in the receptacle only apply, in the opinion of this board, if an agreement had been arrived at between the operator or manager and the person offering the grain for sale that the grain be purchased.
In other words, this interpretation gives the right to the elevator agent to say to the farmer: "I refuse to purchase your grain". Under that ruling I have mentioned, unless the two parties agree that the grain is to be purchased the farmer has no alternative but to accept the price offered or take his grain home. In other words by one stroke of the pen the protection that has been in

the Canada Grain Act for years has been removed by this judgment of the board of transport commissioners. I think it is a judgment that is wrong in every way. I do not think it is based on the facts of the case, and I do not believe such a board should attempt to vary the clear provisions of the Canada Grain Act.
With the right which the farmer has had for many years gone it seems to me that my argument is strengthened in advocating the adoption of such a measure as Bill No. 186, which would set up a fair method for distribution of box cars amongst elevator companies. I believe the arrangement is workable. If the farmers indicate that 60 per cent of the box cars should go to a certain company because 60 per cent of the farmers with 60 per cent of the acreage want to deliver their grain to that company, then I think the railway agent should see to it that 60 per cent of the box cars are spotted at that particular elevator. 1 do not see anything standing in the way of such a provision in the act working smoothly indeed.
In any discussions I have had with people who are conversant with the Canada Grain Act, and the marketing of grain in western Canada, only one other idea has been advanced as perhaps equal to the idea contained in this bill. That was the idea that the elevator agents should each day report to the railway company their purchases of grain, and that the future spotting of box cars should be based on the daily purchases of grain by the various elevator agents. There is only one thing wrong with that idea, and that is that if you start in the fall with two elevators each of which is empty, you will have one of the elevator companies-the one to which most farmers wish to deliver-fill up quite rapidly; then of course the box cars will come in first of all to that company which has been buying grain. But before the elevator company that had its house filled first gets any box cars at all, the second elevator house will be filled. Hence you would have each of them entitled to the same number of box cars even though farmers preferred one elevator company to the other.
As I have said, I think another advantage provided by this bill is the fact that it will restore competition in the buying of grain. Right now there is little effective competition in the purchasing of grain. It used to be that there was real competition in grain buying, a fact which affected grades and consequently prices. But when a farmer comes to town now and finds all the elevators filled but one, the chances are that he will take his grain to that elevator company and will be
Canada Grain Act
obliged to accept whatever grade may be offered for that grain.
Another reason I recommend the bill to the house is that I feel it is a satisfactory alternative to the car order book, and that as long as the car order book is not in effect the provisions of this bill would provide for the allocation of box cars on a basis that would result in a great deal less friction among the farmers and among the elevator companies concerned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a simple, straightforward bill and I think the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) has made a good case in support of it.
I am therefore going to say what I have to say in a very few words.
First of all I may say that we in the Social Credit group intend to support it because we favour the general principle that I think is embodied in the bill, namely that a farmer should have the right to deliver his grain to an elevator of his own choice. I realize that many people will say that a farmer already has that right. While it is true that in theory he does have that right, in actual practice it unfortunately does not work out that way.
At many points we find that the majority of farmers desire to deliver their grain to one specific elevator, maybe because it represents a certain company or maybe because the elevator agent at that elevator has given exceptionally good service. Hence when the crops are harvested we find that the majority of grain starts to come in to that elevator, with the result that it becomes plugged early in the season. Then the farmers are left with the option of either holding their grain or hauling it to other elevator companies.
Then we find that in years of congestion, when the elevators become plugged, it has often been the practice in the past to allocate box cars on the basis of the storage capacity of the various elevators, regardless of the fact that the only reason some of the elevators are full is that the farmers could not haul their wheat anywhere else if they wanted to get it in. We feel that the box cars should be allocated in proportion to the amount of wheat the farmers desire to deliver to any one elevator. In other words, if the farmers desire to deliver 70 per cent of their grain to any one elevator, that elevator should be receiving 70 per cent of the box cars.
I notice that a proposal similar to this was supported by the convention of the Alberta wheat pool delegates. We believe that it will provide for a fairer distribution of the box cars and will help to provide for the practical application of the principle that a

Canada Grain Act
farmer should have the right to deliver his grain to an elevator of his own choice. We therefore propose to support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this bill. From time to time I have had many letters from farmers complaining about having to take their grain to an elevator which they did not wish to patronize. The explanatory note opposite page 1 of the bill reads:
The purpose of this act is to provide in a new section of the car order book a rule for the fair allocation of box cars among elevator companies at a marketing point where the car order book, as presently constituted, is not in effect. By allocating their seeded acreage among the elevator companies at a marketing point, producers themselves will determine the distribution of box cars at that point.
I think if the farmers indicate where they are going to sell their grain and so notify the elevator companies, then the box cars can be allocated on an acreage basis, and you will not have a farmer going around looking for somewhere else to sell his grain at the same point. That is, when there are six elevators and one of the elevators is doing 50 per cent of the business, it should have more cars than the other ones. As it is today, where there are six elevators and six cars come along, they get one apiece. The upshot is that the farmer who patronizes the elevator that is getting 50 per cent of the grain is obliged to go and sell his grain elsewhere.
The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) explained the matter well. I do not need to go into it again and repeat what he has already said. I think this is the solution to the problem which the farmer has today with a glutted market, and I support the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to take only a moment or two in connection with this proposed legislation. I think the first thing I would say is that I would consider the last two or three years as rather abnormal years in so far as crops in western Canada are concerned.
I think I am correct in saying that at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool delegates last November or December a proposal similar to this was brought forward, and I think I am correct in saying that it was voted down. The reason for that, if I might suggest it, was that it would rob the grower of his rights under other sections of the act.
The present act gives the grower the right to order a car for the shipment of his grain and to direct where such car should be spotted, elevator or platform. I doubt whether any farmer would wish to give up this right. While this bill proposes to provide

a new section in the act, care should be taken that the actual result is not to abrogate the right now given to growers. One of the greatest rights the farmer now has is the right to bargain under section 111 of the act for the grade of his grain and for other conditions under which he might deliver it. It would appear that this right to bargain and to change his mind about where he delivers his grain would be effectively lost if this bill were accepted.
I think this bill should have extremely careful consideration. Possibly at the next session consideration should be given to a bill of this kind at the meetings of the standing committee on agriculture.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
if the committee on agriculture is not called any more regularly in future than it has been called recently, I am afraid we would be a long time in getting any necessary amendments to the Canada Grain Act. I had not intended to speak because I believed the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) had covered the matter fully, and I agreed with his argument. But the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater), in the speech which he made, indicated that if this amendment were passed it would abrogate the right of the growers at the present time with regard to the car order book. That is not correct, and I wish to correct him. Section 72B of part I of the bill deals with that and states quite definitely:
If, at any time, no unfilled application for a car appears in the car order book at a marketing point, the railway agent shall then apportion railway cars among the elevator companies in the proportion that the acreage has been divided among the elevator companies.
In other words, if the growers at a point Which has a car order book wish to continue that method they can do so. If they fail to use the car order book, then this other method, as indicated in Bill No. 186, will go into effect.
The car order book was put into effect originally to give the farmer a chance to get a car, as opposed to the elevator companies. It was put in there a great many years ago. It was put in the act before we had the pools in operation and before we had the farm grain companies in operation. It was put into effect before we had the quota system of deliveries, and it served a real purpose; but that purpose has been more or less superseded by the new conditions that have arisen in the last few years with regard to quota deliveries, and the fact that in western Canada today we have in operation certain grain companies which belong to the farmers, co-operatives and so on.

It is the desire of the farmers, instead of using the loading platforms, to use their own companies. Yet at the present time they are not able to do that. This bill would just give them back the right they had under the car order book, when it was first placed in the Canada Grain Act. It is a good bill, and it should be passed.

speechtext: I would first like to correct the grain statistics put on the record by the proposer of this bill. If his statistics are correct I do not see how anyone would have the conscience to demand a maximum price of $2.05 per bushel for wheat. He says that there are two and one half years' supply of wheat stored today in the world. That is perfect nonsense, of course.

speechtext: See your own publications.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext:
He also says the Canadian carryover next year will be 350 million bushels of wheat. That again is nonsense. The fact of the matter is that North America had very big crops last year. We are moving ours as fast as we can get transportation. We have already sold from this crop more than our usual export from a normal crop of wheat. If we could move our wheat faster we would sell more. The difficulty is in transportation rather than in sales. But it is my opinion, and I think the opinion of responsible men around the world, that the reserve stocks of wheat are not more than reasonable protection against the vagaries of nature.
It must be remembered that this continent has had seven or eight years of abnormally large crops. The law of averages works over a period, and we are due at any time for a short crop. I may say that moisture conditions over the prairies this year are not too promising. To tell the world that this great surplus exists is an invitation to sell the market down. I do not know whether my hon. friend intended it that way, but I think any grain man, if he believed my hon. friend's statistics, would not be buying wheat at $2.05, or anywhere near that price.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext: That is your interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR FAIR ALLOCATION OF BOX CARS
speechtext:
You gave us your own interpretation of the statistics. I think the grain men would analyse the position a little more closely.
However, we are discussing the provisions of this bill. It is quite correct to say that the car order book was designed for a different purpose from the one it serves today. It was introduced at a time when there was an open market, when the elevators were privately-owned, when many farmers felt
Canada Grain Act
they would prefer to load over a loading platform rather than patronize one of the privately-owned elevators. It was believed by the farmers that grain that had been bought by the private elevator companies was sent forward in preference to farmer-owned grain, in order to take advantage of premium markets.
The car order book was introduced so that everyone would have an equal chance in the distribution of box cars. I may say that it corrected a situation that badly needed to be corrected at that time, and it served a very useful purpose. Today the car order book is not used in many sections of Canada. It is used in others and still performs a useful service; nevertheless the purpose of using it today is to favour certain elevator companies rather than to avoid discrimination between individuals.
It is felt that if a long list of priorities could be established for any one elevator, that elevator will have preference over neighbouring elevators in the distribution of box cars, and that is so. The suggestion has been made that with five elevators at a point and cars being put into that point, each elevator gets one car, but that only the elevator that has the greatest list of requisitions gets the preference in the cars. As a matter of fact, and generally speaking the usual preference is that a pool elevator will get two cars to one car for any privately-owned elevator. I think that is the usual average.
I was told that that is about the usual average when a string of box cars are being spotted at any particular elevator point.
However, it is now proposed that the distribution of box cars will be made absolutely rigid by law. It is assumed that those who wish to register their seeded acreage will do so. If all the seeded acreage were registered from one elevator, that one elevator would do all the business and the others would do no business at all. That assumes, of course, that we have far too many country elevators on the prairies; that there are five elevators at a given point but four of them are useless. One elevator can do all the work if the farmers "wish to patronize that one elevator. That of course is an absurd premise. I do not think we have too many country elevators. I do think that all of them are needed.
The fact of registering seeded acreage at a point freezes the farmer to the elevator with which he has registered his seeded acreage. If he puts his grain into an elevator other than the one in which he has registered his seeded acreage, obviously he can get no box cars for his grain because he has

Canada Grain Act
specified in advance that the box cars must be spotted at the elevator where his seeded acreage is registered. It takes away his flexibility of delivery and in that way attempts to make a rigid distribution of box cars, which may very well not suit the conditions of the crop movement.
To use the seeded acreage as a basis is by no means reasonable in every season. It is true that the wheat board uses the seeded acreage as a basis for quota purposes. That basis may be changed. If it were changed this whole bill would become null and void. It is tied absolutely to the theory that the seeded acreage will continue to be the basis for quotas used by the wheat board. Seeded acreage is no legal basis for anything. It is simply a device used by the wheat board to establish quotas reasonably fairly over western Canada.
I cannot see that this bill would assist the situation in any way. We have appointed a transport controller to operate our transportation system in times of congestion, his purpose being to make sure that the distribution of box cars is as fair as he can make it. I think that by using his own judgment the transport controller has created a flexible system which has served the farmers well. Many farmers will testify that if they write the transport controller and say that a particular area of which they have knowledge is congested, he will immediately ask the railways to relieve that particular area.
I am firmly of the opinion that any rigidity such as is imposed by this bill, which makes it mandatory on the railways to follow the principles laid down in the bill, regardless of any local situation, would not be satisfactory. There might be grain spoiling at one point, or in one elevator, and the law would say, "You cannot give box cars to that elevator, because under the law as laid down by this bill you must give it to the elevator for which the seeded acreage would make it mandatory."
I am always willing to support legislation which I think will improve the situation in western Canada, either improve the distribution of box cars, or improve any other condition that has to do with the movement of grain to the terminals. As the minister who is responsible for the marketing of grain it is in the interests of the job I am attempting to do to see that we move grain to the terminals in the most efficient manner.
I am not going back on the purpose of the car order book. The purpose of the car order book has always been to assist individuals. This bill makes it a device to assist elevator companies in a way which

Whether it is wise in the interests of supporting one elevator company as against another elevator company to put that rigidity in the law, my hon. friend may have his own opinions. But I am firmly of the opinion that that is not a wise extension of the car order book privilege. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move in amendment:
That the word "now" be left out, and the words "this day six months hence" be added to the end of the question.

member for The Battlefords (Mr. Bater) and the minister have raised a lot of straw men, and then have attempted to knock them down. The minister has said that this would provide a great amount of rigidity in the Canada Grain Act, in the method of allocating box cars. Is there anything more rigid than the present car order book, when the next car coming to a given marketing point on a certain day must be spotted at a certain elevator for shipment of wheat from a certain individual farmer? The present car order book is the most rigid system one could possibly imagine.
I am not complaining about its rigidity. I think that even with the rigidity attached to the car order book it has an important place to fill in the marketing of our grain. The formula I am asking to have applied would apply not all the time but only when the car order book is not being used. It would not take any right away from any producer. But when the car order book is not being used, then this particular formula, as a result of indications given by the producers themselves, would be used in the allocation of box cars.
The minister has said that perhaps grain would be spoiling at a certain marketing point. This provision does not prevent cars going to that particular marketing point. It says that when they do go to that marketing point they must be distributed on a certain basis. I can imagine the arguments against this formula being used each and every day, and can judge perhaps better than the minister could judge.
There is a provision in the Canada Grain Act-and I refer specifically to section 68 (2)- which gives the board the right to alter even the car order book formula on a temporary basis if it thinks an inequality has resulted. While I am not a lawyer, I would be quite prepared to have that paragraph applied to the whole of the Canada Grain Act, as I think it would, anyway; because if one elevator were empty it would not need 40 per cent of the box cars. I understand that. But the chances of an elevator house

becoming empty under the present situation are, in my opinion, almost impossible.
The situation is that you have plugged elevators; and when an elevator has room for 4,000 bushels of wheat, in a day or two there will be 6,000 bushels in front of the elevator house waiting to be unloaded. The farmers do not find the elevators empty. They sometimes find when they go to town with a load of grain that they have to take it home because there is no space.
Then the minister says that if there are six elevator companies at one point it is not right to say that cars are now distributed one to each company. Well, I think that method is used more often than the method of giving the pool two cars for each one that the other elevators companies are getting. We have the car order book in effect now at dozens of country marketing points. Because the pool elevator is sponsoring the use of the car order book, it feels it has been discriminated against in the allocation of box cars.
Then the minister says:	Supposing there
are four elevator companies at a marketing point. The farmers can decide to sell their grain to one, and there are three elevator companies which do not buy any grain. He says that surely we do not think there are top many elevator houses in western Canada. My answer is that if there are four elevator houses at one point, and all the farmers want to deliver their grain to the one elevator, then the other three elevators should go out of business or should sell to the one to which the farmer wishes to deliver his grain.
Surely that is the way competition works. Surely that is free enterprise. If the farmers do not wish to deliver to three elevator companies, but wish to deliver to only one of them, then under ordinary competition the one would buy out the other three and use the four elevator houses. They would all be in use, and the farmers would have the opportunity to deliver their grain to the elevator of their own choice.
I am happy to go along with everything the minister said concerning the effective work done by the transport controller in connection with the relieving of congestion. I think his allocation of box cars in the areas requiring box cars is a good one. But the transport controller does not allocate the box cars among the elevator companies at grain marketing points. He merely says, "Here is a marketing point which requires 20 cars. We would like to see those 20 cars go to that marketing point." In other words, the transport controller does not know any more than I do which elevator companies will get those 20 box cars.

I know from practical experience that in certain instances this would help the line elevators, where they might have a popular agent or where farmers believed in that method of marketing. speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GRANT OF CERTAIN TAXES TO CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to discuss the principle having to do with the manner in which the finances of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will be raised. I think perhaps, in introduction of the few remarks I have to make, I might call to the attention of the committee the statement which was made by my colleague the Minister of Finance on the occasion of the presentation of his budget speech. As reported at page 2133 of Hansard he said, among other things:
The government has been seeking a fair and effective source of revenue for the national system of television broadcasting being developed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in accordance with the general policy that was announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The government's policy is to have the cost of the national television service paid, as far as that is practicable, by those who benefit from such service. It also wishes the C.B.C. to have a direct source of revenue, on which it can budget over a period, and not to be dependent upon annual appropriations to finance its operations. We wish to emphasize that it is a separate corporate body, under the general control of parliament but not a part of the government.
Television operations have just recently commenced and their development has been financed by loans specifically authorized in the estimates. It is now expected that, in addition to commercial television revenues, the C.B.C. will require about $6 million in the next fiscal year to meet operating costs of television, including interest on loans. This requirement will increase over the next few years, perhaps to about $10 million. Some part of these needs during the development period may properly be met from loans, and paid from future revenues, but we should start now with a plan to provide adequate revenues over the long run.
It is therefore proposed that the Canadian Broadcasting Act should be amended to provide that the corporation should in future receive from month to month the amount of revenue yielded by the present 15 per cent special excise tax on television sets and the picture tubes for such sets, and on such parts and accessories for television sets as are taxable under the Excise Act. In this way those who buy sets, or the replacement tubes for them, will be providing the basic revenue necessary for C.B.C. television services. In order to make this plan effective, it will be necessary to revise the regulations to provide that tourists returning to Canada may not include as baggage eligible for free entry television sets or the picture tubes for use in them.
Having decided upon this plan in regard to television, we have now come to the conclusion that a similar transfer of the 15 per cent special excise tax revenue can and should be made to assist in financing radio broadcasting,-
That is, of course, sound broadcasting.
-in place of the present licence fee. Although the continuation of this fee had been recommended by

Canadian Broadcasting Act the Massey commission, experience has convinced us that it is uneconomical to collect such a small individual fee from such a high proportion of Canadian families, if any satisfactory alternative is open. We believe that payment to the C.B.C. of the amount of revenue received from the 15 per cent special excise tax on radio sets and the taxable parts and accessories for them does provide a satisfactory alternative, at least for the next few years until the present statutory grant for radio broadcasting is reviewed at the end of its five-year term. Consequently we are proposing that the broadcasting act should provide for this transfer of revenue, as well as that for television, and that the order in council under the Radio Act setting the present licence fees of $2.50 should be revoked with effect from April 1.
Of course all members of the committee are aware of the fact that the Radio Act was amended yesterday, and that amendment which discontinues the $2.50 fee is in effect from April 1. The Minister of Finance continued:
I estimate that the amount of revenue to be received by the C.B.C. under these arrangements will be approximately $12 million in the next fiscal year, the amount in respect of radio probably exceeding somewhat that for television. The public will be relieved of paying something over $6 million in radio licence fees, this next fiscal year, and our expenditure in collecting such fees, anticipated at $700,000 in the estimates, will be saved.
I have just a few words of explanation to give with reference to the procedure that has been followed since that budget speech was made. The Department of National Revenue, which collects the excise tax, early in March sent out instructions to dealers that return of taxes should in the future be separate as between radio and television. Our previous custom was to lump the two together. The March tax on those sets which have been sold is not due until the end of April. These figures when they are received must be tabulated and analysed. It is expected therefore that it will not be until the end of May or early in June that accurate figures can be given as to the excise tax revenue for radio and television separately.
Unit sales, based on the ten months of 1952 and estimated for a full year, of radio units was 501,974; television units 102,844, and record players, 24,546. The excise tax collected upon combined radio and television products for the year 1951-52 was $8,252,000. During that period sales of radio products were higher than those of television. However, based on bureau of statistics figures for the first ten months of 1952, it is estimated that the sales of each of these products are about equal. Sales for this period were approximately $38 million each for radio and television; that is $78 to $80 million for both. Therefore it is reasonable to assume that the revenue from excise tax in each of these divisions will be equal. The estimated excise tax for combined radio and television 
for the year 1952-53 is about $10,500,000. This figure is based upon a ten-month period.
Yesterday the committee on radio broadcasting paid a visit to and had a meeting in the city of Toronto. They were able to have a close-up view and study of the facilities which we have in that city, and actually see the production of a television program. All hon. members found that very interesting and illuminating. It did give them a concept of the enormous expenditure that is necessary to equip a station, both from the point of view of capital expenditure and yearly maintenance. It gave them a splendid idea of where the taxpayers' money went, and how expensive it is to carry on these operations.
I have nothing further to say except to answer any questions which may be asked on the resolution. If we proceed from the resolution stage to the second reading of the bill containing the amendments which will be made to the broadcasting act, it is my intention to move that the bill be referred to the special committee on broadcasting. The bill just provides that:
The Minister of Finance shall from time to time grant to the corporation out of the consolidated revenue fund amounts that, in the opinion of the Minister of National Revenue, are equal to the taxes collected under part XI of the Excise Tax Act in respect of the goods mentioned in section 6, schedule I to that act.

Mr. Chairman, as the minister has indicated, this resolution follows logically upon the decision taken by the house yesterday in amending the Radio Act to abolish the $2.50 fee on radio receiving sets, a decision taken with unanimous approval of the house, a decision welcomed I am sure by all, a decision long years overdue.
This present measure is, as I understand it, designed now to fill the gap created by yesterday's amendment of the Radio Act, and to provide alternative revenue to meet the needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. That need relates to the activities of the corporation with respect to both sound broadcasting and the development of television which is now just beginning.
The estimate that was made by the Minister of Finance as to the revenue which would be available under the proposed measure was $12 million. That has been broken down a little more closely since that time to these figures: anticipated revenue from the excise tax on television sets and picture tubes, $6 million; that from radio receiving sets and tubes approximately $5,750,000. It happens that the sum of $5,750,000 is the amount that was previously yielded to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by the $2.50 fee on radio receiving sets. This measure, therefore, if adopted will give to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, it is estimated, almost exactly the same revenue for its sound broadcasting activities as it is losing by the repeal of the $2.50 licence fee.
As to television, as the committee appreciates, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in all it has done up to the present time with respect to television has operated entirely on loans from parliament. Those loans, sir, have aggregated altogether $8 million. The first loan was $4,500,000. Then there was a second in 1950 of $1,500,000; then last year, 1952, parliament voted another $2 million loan, making in all $8 million.
The present measure, as I understand it, will put an end to the policy of loans. It will then be the duty of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in its television operations, on their financial side, to make provision for the repayment of those loans according to the terms agreed upon between the corporation and the government at the time those loans were made.
It may be an ingenious scheme that the Minister of Finance put forward. It may be that it is a striking coincidence that the amount expected to be yielded from the excise tax on radio receiving sets and tubes happens to be almost exactly the same as the amount hitherto received from the $2.50 licence fee on radio receiving sets. But, Mr. Chairman,
Canadian Broadcasting Act I think we will have to look a little more deeply into and beyond these superficial and rather striking coincidences in amounts.
As I understand it, it is the duty of parliament, in reference to the voting of money, to assert and to maintain strict control over parliamentary appropriations and expenditures. When the amendment of 1951 was before the house and the house was asked to vote for a period of five years an annual sum of $6,250,000 for the general financial purposes of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, those of us in this part of the house said that the principle of voting money for a five-year period in advance was fundamentally wrong. Whatever might be said for the parliamentary grant to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-and no one took objection to the grant for the year then under consideration-that was no argument whatever for a five-year grant, in advance, without any necessity of the matter being referred back to parliament year by year within that period of time.
The position we took at that time was fundamentally sound; and the majority of the house, in deciding by legislation that that matter would be placed beyond the reach of parliament for a period of five years, in my submission failed in its duty with reference to parliamentary control over public expenditures.
The measure now before us apparently is designed to repeat the same error. It may be well to ask parliament to make this sum available this year. Parliament has control of the matter, parliament has the facts before it, and parliament can act this year. It would not then be tying its hands for the future- next year, or the year after, or the third year or the fourth year. But if we are to follow the statement made by the Minister of National Revenue this evening, and read again what was said by the Minister of Finance on February 19 as reported at page 2133 of Hansard, apparently this present measure is to have effect for at least the same period as the five-year statutory grants which, thus far, have run only two years.
If that is the effect of the measure, then I say another error is being made. Because whatever may be said for these grants at the present time, it is of fundamental importance in the discharge of our duty as a parliament that we should not give away the right or attempt to pass off the obligation we owe to maintain supervision over this grant year by year.
There may be additional reasons why the matter should be reviewed each year. If the figures with which we have been furnished
4188	HOUSE OF
Canadian Broadcasting Act are borne out by experience, it happens that this year there is a quite close similarity between the amount the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is losing by reason of the repeal of the $2.50 licence fee and the amount they are to receive through the excise tax on radio receiving sets and tubes. But that equation may not exist in the following year, or the year after that.
If I understood correctly what the minister said this evening, as well as the remarks of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, we are to be invited to say, by way of legislation, that for the period of five years, or what remains of it, this is the grant to be made; and the matter will not have to be referred back to parliament year by year. If that is the effect of it, then I think the house is being invited by the government to commit another serious mistake.
The finances of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are of very great importance. Its operations are highly important, particularly at this time when it has entered upon the new field of television broadcasting. It would be a very indiscreet man indeed who would attempt to weigh the full influence and effect of television. It is a new and potent force; it is a force which enters into the homes of the nation, and will exert an influence far beyond the ability of any of us now here to comprehend. It will exert an influence upon the thinking of old and young alike in a way that has not been experienced before.
Nothing, then, could be more important in the discharge of our parliamentary duties to the nation and to its homes than that there should be frequent review of the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and its administration. It has been the policy of the House of Commons, since the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was first established, to have a committee of the house review its operations every two years. As a matter of fact, sometimes the period has been longer than two years; but in this post-war period the interval has been about two years, on a strict average.
In connection with the voting of large sums such as are involved in this bill-$12 million per annum; and perhaps more than that in the future-I say there should be an annual review. I am not saying that the committee must be set up every year. It may or may not be decided by the house, in its wisdom, to set it up every year in the future. It may continue to follow the policy of biennial committees. But when we are dealing with an amount like $12 million in relation to the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting 

Corporation, both with respect to sound broadcasting and television, then I say it is highly important that the voting of this money should come before the house every year.
If we are to follow the procedure indicated by the minister this evening, and as foreshadowed by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech on February 19, then we are putting it beyond our reach to touch this matter for the period of the five years during which the other annual parliamentary grants have effect, and without any further vote on the part of parliament. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation under this measure will enter the new fiscal year with revenues of about $22 million. Of that, $15 million is to be used in sound broadcasting and $7 million in television. Of that $7 million, we see that $6 million will come under this bill and approximately $1 million, it is anticipated, from commercial revenues. These are large amounts; and if parliament is to do its duty then, in my submission, it should review these amounts annually.
The argument has been used-it was used in 1951 when we said that these grants should not be voted for five years in advance-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation needed assured revenue in order to carry out long-term planning. I am as appreciative as any member of the necessity for long-term planning in the field of sound broadcasting and that of television. In the committee on broadcasting we have been hearing a description of the plans of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in that regard. No one wishes to tie their hands in making plans, but parliamentary control should first be vindicated. I think the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can have sufficient confidence in parliament and its desire to see that adequate provision is made to meet the proper expenses of the corporation to be assured that year by year parliament will provide what is shown to be required for the purposes approved by parliament.
While recognizing the necessity of providing revenue to replace that lost by the corporation as a result of the abolition of the $2.50 licence fee; while admitting the specious attraction of the present proposal which has some ingenious aspects; while recognizing that so far as may be possible the burden should be borne by those who enjoy the benefits, nevertheless I see in the present proposal something more than just a convenient way of making the necessary provision. If I understand what has been proposed,
I see here something that may be entitled to command the approval of parliament this year, but something which invites

parliament improperly to tie its hands in future years. That should not be done.

the second reading of Bill No. 316, relating to trade marks and unfair competition.
He said: Mr. Speaker this bill revises and consolidates the Unfair Competition Act, 1932 (22-23 George V, c. 39), which has been in force since September 1, 1932, and other statutory provisions relating to trade marks, trade names and acts of unfair competition. As, the main subject dealt with is trade marks, the short title provided for in section 1 of the bill is the Trade Marks Act.
As many criticisms had been directed against the provisions of the Unfair Competition Act, 1932, and their interpretation and application had given rise to such dissatisfaction, in the fall of 1947 the then secretary of state entrusted to an advisory committee of experts in this field of law the task of studying the representations and suggestions already submitted, of securing further views from organizations and individuals who might appear to have an interest in the matter, and of making recommendations for the drafting of new legislation or, if deemed advisable, submitting a draft statute for consideration. In addition to legal practitioners specializing in, amongst other fields, the law of trade marks, and officials administering the Unfair Competition Act, the said committee included representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the patent institute of

Canada. More recently an official of the Department of Justice has also taken part in the committee's work.
At an early stage of the committee's work questionnaires were distributed to and representations received from interested persons and bodies in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, including the patent institute of Canada, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the board of trade of the city of Toronto, the law society of Upper Canada, the United States trade mark association, the chartered institute of patent agents of the United Kingdom and the trade marks, patents and designs federation of the United Kingdom. Copies of the questionnaires were distributed to their membership by the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the patent institute of Canada and the Association of Canadian Advertisers Incorporated. A questionnaire was also published in the Canadian Bar Review and in the Ontario Weekly Notes. Notice of the activities of the committee was published in the journal of the patent office society of the United States, and mention of its work and objects was made in the daily press of Canada.
The committee has been in contact with other departments of the government of Canada having an interest in some of the proposed provisions, namely the Departments of Trade and Commerce, of national revenue (customs and excise) and of finance, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the statute revision commission and the Criminal Code revision commission.
The committee has had an average of half a dozen meetings a year over a period of approximately five years. A considerable amount of work was done and time devoted to the committee's task between those meetings by subcommittees or individual members of the committee. Nearly two years ago it produced a first printed draft of the bill, which it circulated amongst substantially the same organizations and individuals who had received the questionnaires, more particularly those who had indicated an interest in the subject, and which it also made available to any others who signified a desire to receive copies. Further representations were received as a result, either indicating general approval of that first draft or containing helpful criticisms and suggestions for improvement.
The same treatment was accorded to the latter submissions as had been accorded to those received by the committee upon the questionnaires circulated by it at the beginning of its work; that is, they were carefully considered and any suggestions that

appeared to the committee to be reasonable and helpful were adopted and incorporated in the committee's draft, which was submitted to parliament in the Senate in June, 1952. Subsequently further representations were received, some of which appeared to have merit, and some amendments were made and incorporated in the bill which was introduced in the Senate earlier in the present session.
I hope the foregoing will not give the impression that we pretend to have produced a bill which meets all views. On a branch of the law which is of such a technical character, and at the same time of such practical importance to commerce, industry and the legal profession, it is obviously impossible to achieve unanimity of opinion on all points and proposals. It is for these very reasons that it was intended to afford all concerned an opportunity to give full consideration to, and make representations on, this bill.
The committee has prepared a detailed explanatory report which has been printed and published. Such report may prove very useful later in the administration and interpretation of the new legislation, if adopted. One precedent for this is the Goschen report on the 1938 legislation relating to trade marks in the United Kingdom.
May I, at this point, take occasion to pay well-merited tribute to the valuable services rendered by the trade marks law revision committee who, over a period of nearly six years, have given of their services unstintingly, attended many meetings and devoted many days of their time to this work entirely without remuneration.
I should now like briefly to summarize the main changes that this bill would bring about in the existing law as follows:
1.	The elimination of the arbitrary division of trade marks into word marks and design marks, introduced by the Unfair Competition Act, 1932.
2.	A more adequate definition of what constitutes a trade mark in the light of modern commercial practice.
3.	The applicability of trade marks to services in addition to wares.
4.	Relaxation of the rigid rules applying to the assignment and licence of trade marks.
5.	Clarification of the principles governing the ownership of trade marks in Canada and the persons entitled to registration, including the right to file an application for registration prior to commencing actual use.
6.	Provision for publication of trade mark applications and for opposition procedure.
7.	In addition, an effort has been made to gather, into a compendious whole, the provisions contained in various statutes providing
Trade Marks Act
prohibitions against adoption and use of marks and symbols such as, for example, the insignia of the Boy Scouts, insignia of the armed forces and university emblems.
I should add that special care has also been taken to ensure that the provisions of the bill were in accord with Canada's obligation under the convention of the union of Paris for the protection of industrial property, including its London, 1934, amendments to which Canada adhered in 1951.
It is my intention, if the bill is given second reading, to move that it be referred to the committee on banking and commerce.

EMERGENCY POWERS ACT-ORDER IN COUNCIL RE TRADE WITH MAINLAND CHINA AND NORTH KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one matter I should like to place before the house before we go into supply. It has to do with the order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act which was tabled in the house yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). He brought in this order in council, which is No. 604, shortly before the noon recess. It is described as the "Control of trade by sea with mainland China and North Korea, order 1953".
The terms of this order in council are very far-reaching. In the first place it sets up what is a completely new licensing system for Canadian ships. As hon. members know, there are already various licences and certificates required by Canadian ships; but here we have an order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act which sets up a completely new and additional licensing system. That provision is found in paragraph 3 of the order which reads as follows:
3 (1) No Canadian ship to which this order applies shall, on or after the 20th day of April, 1953-
That of course was yesterday. I continue: -proceed to sea from any port (whether within or outside Canada) except under the authority of and in accordance with a licence granted under this order by the minister.
In the definition section of the order in council the minister is defined as the Minister of Transport. Subsection 2 of paragraph 3 reads as follows:
No master, owner or person having the management or control of a Canadian ship shall order, permit or cause any such ship to proceed to sea in contravention of subsection 1.
And by the way, the order is made applicable to every Canadian ship having a gross tonnage of more than 500 tons. It would apply, of course, to both cargo and passenger ships. Paragraph 4 of the order in council goes on further with regard to the licence and reads as follows:
The licence required under this order shall be in addition to any other licence, certificate or authority from time to time required by the law of Canada.

Paragraph 5 reads:
A licence under this order may be general or for a specific voyage or voyages.
Further provisions of the order set out in what ways the minister may limit this licence. Paragraph 6 reads:
Any licence granted under this order may be granted subject to such limitations and conditions as the minister thinks fit to impose with respect to
(a)	the trades in which the ship may engage and the voyages which may be undertaken by the ship;
(b)	the class of cargoes or passengers which may be carried in the ship to mainland China or North Korea or within the territorial waters of those countries;
(c)	the hiring of the ship.
It will be noticed that there for the first time is a reference to mainland China or North Korea, and that is the only reference throughout the whole order in council to these territories.
The wording of the order in council is such that there must be a licence obtained in every case, but then the Minister of Transport may put a limitation or a condition in the licence with regard to the class of cargoes or passengers which may be carried in the ship to mainland China or North Korea, or within the territorial waters of those countries.
I will not read the whole order in council. There are punishment provisions which provide for a maximum fine not exceeding $25,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years or both. In addition there is a provision that a director of a shipping company shall be subject to the same fine or imprisonment if the offence takes place with his knowledge or consent, or even if he fails to exercise due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. The penalty provisions, as hon. members will see, are exceedingly severe.
It should be pointed out that this order in council makes it obligatory for every Canadian ship leaving every port, everywhere- not only in Canada, but leaving port in any other part of the world-if she is over 500 tons, whether passenger or cargo, to obtain a licence under this order in council. The order in council was made applicable at once, without any warning. Obviously it is very far-reaching.
This order in council was passed on April 17, just last Friday, while the House of Commons was in session. No opportunity has been given hon. members to consider it. There was no chance whatever for debate before it became law; there has been no chance for the press of Canada to carry the story of this new law across the country so the people of this nation would have an opportunity to understand what the government was doing.

Trade with China and North Korea
This is the kind of action against which we in the official opposition cannot protest too strongly. Action was taken under the Emergency Powers Act. Hon. members will recall the debates in the house only a few weeks ago in connection with the extension for another year of the provisions of that act. We were led to believe at that time by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that he wanted the Emergency Powers Act continued for another year only as a stand-by power, that the act was required so the government could take whatever steps might be necessary when the house was not sitting.
We were told time and again during the debate that there was no intention to by-pass parliament. Oh, no, there was to he nothing of that kind. This Emergency Powers Act was required merely to do something after we had all gone home. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) said it was needed during the period of the election, because during that time there would be no House of Commons sitting, and that the government required such powers.
Yet the ink on Hansard was scarcely dry when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) walked into the house with a far-reaching order in council of this kind, passed under the Emergency Powers Act. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this action is in defiance of the Canadian parliament, and that it should be treated as such by members of the house and by the Canadian people generally.
Where has democracy gone in this country when a power-mad government will take action of that kind? It is not as though this were the only way the situation could be met. The government could have brought in amendments to the Canada Shipping Act setting up these requirements for a new type of licence. It may be argued that it would have been impossible to draw an amendment to confine the provision to the mainland of China and to North Korea. Yet we have that being done in legislation before the House of Commons at this very time.
I hold in my hand the revised Criminal Code. We find that section 46 thereof deals with treason and other offences against the queen's authority and person. A provision is written into this Criminal Code to deal with a situation such as that existing at this time in North Korea. Leaving aside paragraphs (a) and (b) we find that section 46 (1) (c) states that everyone commits treason who, in Canada-
(c) assists an enemy at war with Canada, or any armed forces against whom Canadian forces are engaged in hostilities whether or not a state of war exists between Canada and the country whose forces they are;

Words of that kind could have been used to amend the Canada Shipping Act to meet the situation dealt with by this order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act.
Then already we have a provision in the Canada Shipping Act to meet a similar situation. I would refer hon. members to the amendments to that act passed in 1938. At that time a section numbered 703A was added. This section is described in the side-note as follows, "prohibition of shipment of articles of war to countries in a state of war." This of course was before the second world war had broken out. We were meeting the problem of the shipping of munitions to potential enemies, and this section was inserted in the Canada Shipping Act at that time.
I make reference to it because I submit that this problem could have been dealt with in the same way by a new section or sections in the Canada Shipping Act. I am not suggesting, of course, that exactly the same wording would have been used. This section 703A provided:
(1) No article to which this section applies shall be discharged at any port or place in any territory designated by the governor in council tor the purposes of this section or within the territorial waters adjacent to such territory from a ship registered in Canada, and no such article shall be transshipped on the high seas from any such ship into any vessel bound for any such port or place, and no such article consigned to or destined for any such port or place shall be taken on board or carried in any such ship.
Then the section went on to give the governor in council-that is, the cabinet-the power from time to time to-
(a)	designate any territory or territories in which there is a state of war or armed conflict, civil or otherwise, in respect of which the provisions of this section shall apply;
(b)	prescribe the time or times during which such provisions shall so apply;
(c)	exempt in the case of any territory so designated any article or class or articles referred to in the next following subsection-
Which makes reference to munitions of war.
-from the application of the provisions of this section;
(d)	provide otherwise for the carrying out of the intent of this section.
Then subsection 3 of section 703A describes the articles to which the section shall apply, and states that they shall include- -arms, ammunition, implements or munitions of war, military, naval or air stores, or any articles deemed capable of being converted thereinto or made useful in the production thereof, or provisions or any sort of victual which may be used as food by man or beast.
There are other subsections of this section which were written into the Canada Shipping Act in 1938.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce says they did the right thing in the wrong way. What has happened is that this government have become so drunk with power that they do not take the trouble to draw up an amendment; they simply come to the floor of the house and throw on the table an order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act and expect members of the House of Commons and the Canadian people to swallow it.
The actual offence is made much worse in that yesterday morning amendments to the Canada Shipping Act were actually being considered. Instead of dealing with them, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) walked out of the house and left his parliamentary assistant to conduct the bill through the house. Another bill amending the Radio Act was treated in the same way and conducted through by the parliamentary assistant. After both bills had been passed the Minister of Transport walked into the house and asked for unanimous consent to revert to motions in order to table this order in council which should have been brought in as an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act, debated and passed in the normal way.
I submit that in this case the government has deliberately by-passed parliament. This sort of high-handed treatment must be stopped. It is time we in Canada knew whether we are to have a free parliament any longer. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house, whilst in accord with a policy of imposing strict limitations and conditions on Canadian ships and cargoes and passengers carried thereon to mainland China or North Korea or within the territorial waters of these countries, desires to record its opinion that the action of the government in proceeding by order in council under the Emergency Powers Act while the house is in session was a violation of the rights of parliament and that any powers necessary to implement such a policy should have been provided by an amendment to the Canada Shipping Act."

The hon. member states that a bill should have been introduced here, passed on to the Senate and sent down the path that any amendment to an existing act must travel. This action to prevent the movement of contraband was not taken by Canada primarily; it was taken by agreement among the NATO countries.
The first action was taken by the United States. Did they pass an act of congress? Not at all; it was done by executive action. The next government to proceed was Great Britain. Was their action taken by means of an act passed through the British parliament? Not at all; it was done by order in council, as we have done it. I cannot be sure of this, but my recollection is that council was told that the order in council passed by the Canadian governor in council was exactly the same as that passed by Britain. Executive action was taken by Greece to stop Greek ships taking part in this trade. As far as I know every NATO country has taken or is in process of taking similar action, in every case by executive action.
This house has given this government a mandate to carry out its responsibilities as one of the NATO countries with forces in Korea. We passed specific legislation authorizing the government to send troops to Korea, to send ships to Korea, to send aircraft to Korea; yet we are told that the endorsement given by the house for that purpose is not broad enough to stop contraband being carried into Korea by Canadian ships. Could anything be more nonsensical than this picayune idea that if we want to stop contraband we cannot do it by executive action? We can send troops to Korea, we can send ships to Korea by executive action; but contraband, no. The contraband must be allowed to continue until the usual processes of this parliament are carried out. If any serious result occurs that is just too bad, but it cannot be helped as the opposition has said, "Let it go until we can put a bill through the house."
My hon. friend has read from the Canada Shipping Act. Are those provisions that require action by the House of Commons? Not at all; they are provisions that require action by the governor in council. We could have passed an order in council under the Canada Shipping Act as the law provides, except for one thing-there has been no 08108-260

We used the Emergency Powers Act because if there ever was a purpose for which the Emergency Powers Act was appropriate, it was meeting a situation that is causing damage to our efforts in Korea. We were told some time ago that there was a growing trade in war materials into red China and something had to be done about it. It is customary when something has to be done in a matter of this kind to do it and not talk about it. My hon. friend is using the Conservative line that has been repeated to us over and over again-you did the right thing, but you did it in the wrong way. How often have we heard that in this parliament. I venture to say it is 50 times.
Here it is again. If my hon. friend gets any comfort out of saying that we did the right thing but in the wrong way, and that is exactly what his amendment says, he is welcome to that comforting statement. We did it in the way every British country is doing it; we did it in the way every other country is doing it-by executive action. If we have overstepped our powers, I make no apology for having done so.
I say we did the right thing in the right way. We did it without too much debate about it, and it is done promptly. Canadian ships will no longer take any part in that trade, although I am happy to say that of the list of ships I saw that had been active in the trade, no Canadian ship was involved.
